Russia’s drones keep targeting the bridges Kyiv can’t easily replace—now the Northern crossing is cratered. Ukraine's government is already weighing earth dams and pontoon crossings in case the city's Dnipro bridges are knocked out.
“Mr Putin, put an end to this senseless war”: Merz in Kyiv, with €1 billion in military aid. The chancellor said Germany is ready for talks, but Russia's attacks on Ukrainian civilians must stop.

“We are staying”: EU embassies remain in Kyiv after Russia warns diplomats to leave or risk their lives. EU Ambassador Katarína Mathernová said Moscow wants to scare Europe into cutting its support for Ukraine, and Poland and Estonia also refused to move.

Ukraine says its strikes have knocked out more than 51% of Russia’s oil refining capacity. Production and procurement of Ukraine's long-range strike drones tripled this year, and the Defense Ministry plans to scale them further.

Comprendre en détail son assurance-groupe L’assurance-groupe se constitue année après année, à partir d’un montant versé par l’employeur. - Shutterstock. S ouscrite par l’employeur pour ses salariés, l’assurance-groupe est un contrat d’assurance. Chaque année, votre patron met de côté un montant, qui peut correspondre à un pourcentage du salaire ou à un montant forfaitaire. Le gouvernement prévoit un rendement minimum de 1,75 %. En dessous de ce taux, l’entreprise doit compléter. Au fil du temps, ces sommes s’accumulent et constituent une réserve de pension, versée automatiquement à l’employé affilié lorsqu’il part à la pension (anticipée). L’argent ne peut pas être retiré avant la retraite. Sauf exceptions. Exemple : lorsqu’un salarié a atteint l’âge légal mais continue à travailler quelques années. Pour qui, pour quoi, comment ? Dans certains secteurs, l’assurance-groupe est obligatoire. Dans la plupart des cas, l’employeur choisit toutefois lui-même d’en souscrire une. « Cet avantage extralégal est répandu en Belgique. Dans le secteur de la construction par exemple, il a été mis en place au niveau sectoriel. Pour les entreprises de plus de 100 personnes, c’est quasi systématique », indique Marc Alen, consultant qui met en place des politiques salariales pour les employeurs chez Acerta. Le montant des cotisations varie notamment selon le statut et le salaire. « En règle générale, l’assurance-groupe est un pourcentage appliqué au salaire annuel brut du travailleur », explique Marc Alen. Les ouvriers peuvent tout autant bénéficier de cet avantage que les salariés. Il donne l’exemple du secteur de la construction : « Le taux de départ pour un ouvrier est de 1,10 %. S’il gagne 45.000 euros par an, cela équivaut à 500 à 600 euros cotisés par an. Un cadre avec un salaire brut annuel double aura un pourcentage six à sept fois supérieur. » Depuis 2015, il n’est plus possible de faire la distinction entre ouvriers et employés dans l’affiliation à une assurance-groupe. Si certaines différences subsistent, elles devront avoir disparu au plus tard en 2030. Pour les indépendants, on parle non pas d’assurance-groupe, mais de PLCI (pension libre complémentaire pour indépendants). Un EIP (engagement individuel de pension) peut également être mis en place par les indépendants qui travaillent via une société. Un complément de pension, mais pas seulement L’assurance-groupe présente plusieurs intérêts pour les employés, notamment sur le plan fiscal. « La pension extralégale obtenue grâce à l’assurance-groupe est, sous la fiscalité actuelle, nettement moins lourdement imposée que le salaire ordinaire », explique Marc Alen. « La taxation du capital épargné par le travailleur pendant sa carrière sera de l’ordre de 15 %, tandis que celle sur un salaire peut monter jusqu’à plus ou moins 45 % », chiffre-t-il. L’assurance-groupe permet de constituer une pension complémentaire et de maintenir un niveau de vie correct à la retraite. Des garanties supplémentaires sont souvent prévues, comme une couverture décès, des intérêts en cas d’incapacité de travail ou une allocation d’orphelin. Pour l’employeur, c’est un élément du package salarial susceptible d’aider à attirer les talents. Fiscalement, l’entreprise peut déduire les primes d’une assurance-groupe comme frais professionnels. Des droits « répertoriés » si je change d’employeur Une démission ou un licenciement ne signifie pas que le capital constitué disparaît. « Les droits acquis ne sont pas perdus, ils sont répertoriés. Les organismes de pension doivent revenir vers leurs affiliés lors de la mise à la retraite avec les informations nécessaires en vue du paiement complémentaire », rassure Mathieu Saudoyer, porte-parole de l’Autorité des services et marchés financiers (FSMA). Deux options s’offrent au salarié : laisser le capital constitué chez l’assureur actuel et continuer à percevoir des intérêts dessus, ou le transférer vers l’assurance-groupe de son nouvel employeur. Pour connaître précisément vos droits, n’hésitez pas à consulter mypension.be et à lire le règlement de pension, c’est-à-dire les règles qui régissent l’assurance-groupe. « La FSMA met également un grand nombre d’informations sur les pensions complémentaires à disposition sur son site web », précise Mathieu Saudoyer. « TF1 et Netflix décident » : Kev Adams évoque l’avenir de la série « Maison de retraite » BelgaImage. Diffusée en mars 2026, « Maison de retraite, la série » ne devrait pas revenir pour une seconde saison. Invité avec Chantal Ladesou sur la chaîne YouTube Censuré ce lundi 5 octobre, Kev Adams a expliqué que le projet était toujours en suspens. De son côté, Chantal Ladesou constate que le succès de la franchise « Maison de retraite » est toujours bien présent auprès du public. Dans les cinémas, elle croise notamment « beaucoup d’enfants, de jeunes » qui lui parlent encore des films et lui demandent régulièrement si un troisième volet verra le jour. À propos de la série, Kev Adams ne cache pas son pessimisme. « A priori non. Ce n’est pas prévu pour l’instant », déclare-t-il à propos d’une saison 2. La saison ne lui appartient pas.« Malheureusement, c’est TF1 et Netflix qui décident », rappelle Kev Adam. Le projet reste donc en suspens : « Pour l’instant, on est en stand-by. Mais le stand-by dure un peu longtemps. » Après deux longs-métrages et une série, un retour au cinéma reste néanmoins possible puisque les deux acteurs n’écartent pas l’idée d’un « Maison de retraite 3 ». Sorti en 2022, le premier film « Maison de retraite » avait rencontré un joli succès. Pour un budget d’un peu moins de 5 millions d’euros, le film avait dépassé les deux millions d’entrées en France. Une suite est sortie, deux ans plus tard. La série a été diffusée par TF1 en mars 2026. Élodie Hesme, Kev Adams et Alice Van Den Broek se sont occupé de la création tandis que TF1 et Netflix ont co-produit les six épisodes. Retrouvez plus d’actualités sur www.soirmag.be et sur Facebook. Jean-François Bourlart dresse le bilan de la saison 2026 de Lotto-Intermarché : « Nos leaders n’ont pas toujours été au rendez-vous » Arnaud De Lie espère terminer son parcours chez Lotto sur une bonne note. - Photo News / Belga Q uand la course s’invite à Binche, c’est un peu le carnaval avant l’heure, une sorte de répétition générale mais en habit d’été puisque celui-ci joue les prolongations. Les deux épreuves hennuyères réservées d’abord aux dames, ensuite aux messieurs sont aussi, souvent, le cadre d’adieux, de passation de pouvoir. C’est là que Philippe Gilbert tira sa révérence au public wallon en 2022. C’était sous le maillot de l’équipe Lotto, comme celui que porte pour quelques jours encore Arnaud De Lie, ancien lauréat sur la place de Binche, en 2024. Jean-François Bourlart, le CEO de l’équipe Lotto-Intermarché avait rêvé d’une saison plus prolifique en ce qui concerne son leader qu’il n’a finalement pas eu le temps de connaître et/ou d’apprivoiser. À lire aussi Quels objectifs pour Evenepoel après son titre européen ? « Tour des Flandres et Tour de France doivent être ses prochains défis », lance Johan Museeuw Jean-François, Binche c’est aussi un peu « votre » course, compte tenu de vos fidèles attaches à votre partenaire Wanty ? Oui, c’est spécial pour nous. Wanty est toujours partenaire de notre équipe de développement et c’est, pour l’entreprise, un jour particulier, comme le sont toutes les épreuves disputées à Binche, d’un départ du Tour de France en passant par les championnats nationaux. Ce sera aussi la dernière course en Wallonie pour Arnaud De Lie sous le maillot de Lotto. Que regard portez-vous sur la saison de votre leader ? Il est en tout cas très motivé pour ce mardi, mais aussi pour Paris-Tours dimanche. Avec lui, tout est toujours possible. Pour le reste, c’est un peu une déception. Sans chercher à qui incombent les responsabilités. Arnaud a rencontré beaucoup de problèmes physiques, étaient-ils liés aux conséquences de sa maladie de Lyme, personne ne peut l’infirmer et le confirmer. Sa saison a été compliquée mais elle n’est pas terminée. Quand le moment sera venu, je lui souhaiterai en tout cas tout le bien pour lui dans son futur chez Tudor. De manière plus globale, comment jugez-vous la saison 2026 de Lotto-Intermarché ? Un sentiment mitigé là aussi car nos leaders n’ont pas été toujours au rendez-vous dans les grandes courses, tels Arnaud et Lennert Van Eetvelt. En revanche, cette situation a permis à certains de se mettre en évidence. C’est le cas de Jenno Berckmoes, qui a gagné en World Tour (étape du Renewi Tour), qui a obtenu une sélection pour les championnats d’Europe. Jenno a une excellente mentalité, il est intelligent et il a pris la dimension d’un leader. Je pense aussi à des éléments comme Simone Gualdi, Steffen De Schuyteneer, Matys Grisel, des jeunes qui ont saisi leur chance. On oublierait que Jarno Widar est le plus jeune d’entre eux ! En effet, après des débuts compliqués et des pépins physiques pour lui aussi, il a donc découvert son premier grand Tour à la Vuelta. J’ai bien aimé sa prestation d’ensemble, animée par l’apprentissage, comme il l’a expliqué plusieurs fois aux médias par rapport au fait qu’il ne jouait pas le général « car je suis ici pour apprendre ». C’est une forme d’intelligence et de maturité. Nous avons prolongé Jarno pour deux années, nous investissons clairement sur lui. Les jeunes ont performé, et des anciens comme Lionel Taminiaux se rappellent à notre bon souvenir… Exact. Je lui ai d’ailleurs dit qu’il avait sa chance à Binche où il a déjà fait troisième (2021). Il est en forme, motivé, et il n’a pas peur de prendre ses responsabilités. Binche sera aussi la course d’adieu d’un vieux serviteur, Jasper De Buyst, onze années chez Lotto et futur responsable de la performance. C’est un beau projet que nous avons élaboré avec lui et je suis content de l’entamer avec un fidèle de la maison Lotto. Le départ d’Aike Visbeek offrait cette possibilité de reconversion à Jasper, un garçon très expérimenté, qui est chaud pour le projet. Il a déjà pris son rôle à cœur avec l’entraîneur et les partenaires techniques. Lotto est actuellement 19 e du classement UCI. Il est prématuré de s’inquiéter ? Non, nous sommes évidemment attentifs à ce classement. Nous serons 7 à 8 équipes concernées pour conserver notre rang en WorldTour au-delà de 2028. Je parle d’équipes qui, comme nous, n’ont pas la possibilité de réaliser de gros transferts mais qui se débrouillent avec les opportunités et leurs jeunes. « Le débat récurrent de l’indemnité de transfert en cyclisme refait surface mais il ne se passe rien et les équipes les plus riches peuvent donc recruter sans s’endetter… » Les départs d’Arnaud De Lie et de Lennert Van Eetvelt seront compensés ? Il n’est pas simple de remplacer deux « leaders » ou qualifiés comme tels mais Clément Venturini, par exemple, s’il ne gagnera jamais le Tour des Flandres peut marquer des points dans des courses comme la Coupe de France où nous ne sommes, d’ordinaire, pas souvent présents. Pour encadrer Jarno Widar, il y aura deux grimpeurs d’expérience avec Guillaume Martin et Mauri Vansevenant. Et pour les sprints, nous offrons à Juan Molano les pleins pouvoirs pour s’exprimer et non à rouler pour l’équipe comme il le faisait chez UAE. Vous saluerez aussi le retour de Stan Dewulf (Decathlon)… C’est un beau renfort pour les classiques, conformément à sa quatrième place au GP de l’E3 au printemps dernier. Avec Jenno Berckmoes et Toon Aerts (rétabli de sa blessure au genou), nous disposerons d’un beau trio dès le début de la saison. Nous n’avons pas van Aert ou van der Poel, mais là encore, on se débrouille. Vous avez également recruté Brandon Fedrizzi, 18 ans, impressionnant avec la sélection italienne aux Mondiaux et aux championnats d’Europe, belle pioche ! Il fera partie de l’équipe de développement mais avec l’idée de l’intégrer au groupe professionnel lorsque la course lui convient, un peu comme l’ont fait Visma avec Brennan ou Ineos avec August. C’est la preuve qu’il est possible, avec certains agents, de ne pas voir tous les talents décelés en junior partir dans les équipes riches. Alex Carrera (NDLR : l’agent, entre autres, de Tadej Pogacar) nous avait déjà proposé Simone Gualdi. Voici maintenant Fedrizzi. C’est une marque de confiance par rapport à notre savoir-faire. A contrario, le jeune Niels Driesen, deuxième du Tour de l’Avenir part chez Pinarello. C’est une déception ? Chaque année, c’est le but, nous avons trois à quatre jeunes qui deviennent professionnels, les agents, là encore, sont bien renseignés. C’est eux qui font la loi et organisent les transferts. Le débat récurrent de l’indemnité de transfert en cyclisme refait surface mais il ne se passe rien et les équipes les plus riches peuvent donc recruter sans s’endetter… Citant Lennert Van Eetvelt ou Arnaud De Lie, ce dernier figurant parmi les favoris ce mardi à Binche, Jean-François Bourlart dresse un bilan mitigé de la saison 2026. Rwandan genocide hunter Dafroza Gauthier dies after long battle for justice. Dafroza Gauthier, who spent spent decades tracking down Rwandans in France accused of involvement in the 1994 genocide, has died from cancer at the age of 72. By filing a string of civil lawsuits against suspected fugitives, she and her husband Alain pushed the French legal system to hold them to account.

France struggles to fund farm climate adaptation as losses mount. Farmers in France are expecting their first payments shortly under the government's billion-euro emergency aid package to support farmers affected by severe summer heatwaves, droughts and wildfires. As the effects of climate change worsen, experts say compensation alone will not be enough to protect French agriculture in the long term.

Ethiopia captures Tigray capital as its regional rivals meet in Egypt. Ethiopian federal forces have regained control of the Tigray rebels' regional capital, local sources said on Sunday, while Ethiopia's regional rivals gathered in Egypt to discuss the risk of a wider war.

The pill: from symbol of women's liberation to subject of growing mistrust. Initially a symbol of liberation, the pill went on to become an almost inevitable part of a woman’s contraceptive journey. But today its use in France is in decline, the drop in popularity fuelled by health warnings, mistrust and a changing attitude towards contraception.

US-German trio win medicine Nobel for work on optogenetics. The Nobel medicine prize was awarded Monday to US psychiatrist and neurologist Karl Deisseroth and his German colleagues Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel for their work in the field of optogenetics.

Nobel Prize announcements begin, with hopes of a 'less controversial year'. With this year's Nobel Prize winner announcements beginning on Monday, among those experts believe could be in line for the $1.2 million prizes are GLP-1 researchers, a Ukrainian children's rights activist and several female authors. And after last year's Donald Trump-driven controversy, anticipation around this year's Peace Prize is high.

France boss Zidane says he is happy with his squad ahead of Belgium test. France boss Zinedine Zidane declared himself happy with his players as they went throught their final preparations for the Uefa Nations League clash against Belgium on Monday night at the Stade de France.

Spain PM calls early election after housing crisis defeat. Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez on Monday called a snap election for 29 November, after parliament rejected housing relief measures proposed by his minority government. This comes after tens of thousands of protesters marched in Madrid and other cities on Saturday to demand affordable housing.

Hundreds of French schools closed as students maintain protest pressure. Nearly 500 highschools across France were closed or partially closed on Monday as students continued their demonstrations over poor learning conditions, ahead of a day of wider protests scheduled for Tuesday.

Study shows extreme poverty, homelessness on the rise in France. An international study published Monday by France’s largest food aid charity Restos du Cœur shows that the number of people living in extreme poverty in France and other wealthy countries, increased by 37 percent between 2018 and 2025.

Chat group kingpin goes on trial in Paris over online abuse of underage girls. A 29-year-old man went on trial on Monday at the Paris Assize Court, charged with running a masculinist chat group on the platform Discord on which young victims were forced to engage in sexual acts online and to mutilate themselves.

Présidentielle au Brésil: «Ce vote est marqué par une forte division de l'électorat». Jour de vote ce dimanche 4 octobre au Brésil pour les élections générales, la présidentielle et les législatives. 158 millions d’électeurs sont convoqués aux urnes pour élire leur président. Ce premier tour de la présidentielle brésilienne oppose 13 candidats dont deux principaux, le président sortant Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva de gauche et le sénateur d'extrême droite Flavio Bolsonaro, fils de l'ancien président Jair Bolsonaro. Quels sont les enjeux de ce scrutin ? João Whitaker, professeur à l’université de São Paulo, est l’invité de la mi-journée de RFI.

Aux États-Unis, de plus en plus de jeunes électeurs noirs se déclarent indépendants. L’un des enjeux pour les démocrates pour les prochaines élections de mi-mandat, c'est de mobiliser les électeurs perdus à la dernière présidentielle, comme les jeunes hommes afro-américains. Donald Trump avait doublé sa part d’électeurs d’hommes afro-américains en 2024, mais de plus en plus de jeunes hommes noirs se déclarent indépendants. Un défi pour les démocrates, qui dans les années 1960 étaient devenus le parti du mouvement des droits civiques.

Bosnie: le dirigeant bosno-serbe Milorad Dodik annonce la victoire de son parti dans la partie serbe. L'ancien dirigeant pro-russe de l'entité serbe de Bosnie-Herzégovine, Milorad Dodik, a déclaré que son parti y avait conservé le pouvoir dimanche lors d'élections générales marquées par une forte baisse du taux de participation.

Élection présidentielle au Brésil: Flavio Bolsonaro devance Lula et l'affrontera au second tour. Au Brésil, le sénateur conservateur Flavio Bolsonaro a créé la surprise dimanche 4 octobre, au premier tour de la présidentielle au Brésil en devançant le président sortant de gauche Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva. Les deux candidats s'affronteront au second tour le 25 octobre.

Blocage des lycées en France: le gouvernement souhaite une reprise des cours où la sécurité le permet. Après une semaine de blocages de lycées marquée par de vives tensions en France, l'exécutif souhaite que les cours reprennent dès lundi 4 octobre partout où la sécurité le permet, et fixe un calendrier pour répondre à une partie des revendications, à la veille d'une journée de mobilisation redoutée.

Sous les frappes russes visant les ponts, Kiev se déplace au ralenti. En Ukraine, Kiev continue de subir des frappes de drones russes sur les ponts qui relient les deux rives de la ville, même pendant la visite du chancelier allemand Friedrich Merz. Si le but de scinder la ville et d'en paralyser les transports n'est pas encore atteint par Moscou, ces attaques perturbent grandement la circulation des résidents, menacés par le Kremlin d'attaques encore plus lourdes.

Vidéo de Raphaël Glucksmann, lycées et LFI: le dernier débat avant la primaire de la gauche sous tension. Les cinq participants à la primaire de la gauche pour désigner un candidat à l'élection présidentielle de 2027 se sont retrouvés dimanche sur BFMTV pour un dernier débat. Pendant plus de trois heures, Olivier Faure, Raphaël Glucksmann, Jérôme Guedj, Emmanuel Maurel, Ségolène Royal se sont affrontés dans des échanges souvent tendus, avec en préambule des questions brûlantes sur les propos embarrassants de Glucksmann dans une vidéo publiée la veille à l'insu du candidat.

Inde: la mobilisation pour «sauver la démocratie» se poursuit et promet de grandir encore. La colère ne faiblit pas en Inde. Pour le quatrième jour consécutif ce lundi 5 octobre, la rue se mobilise pour « sauver la démocratie », alors que la journée de dimanche a déjà été intense, notamment dans la capitale. Avec comme cible de la contestation le chef de la Commission électorale, Gyanesh Kumar, toujours soupçonné d'avoir orchestré la suppression de 130 millions d’inscrits sur les listes électorales à l'avantage du BJP de Narendra Modi.

Pakistan: Islamabad se barricade pour empêcher les partisans d'Imran Khan d'entrer dans la capitale. Après l’échec de négociations entamées vendredi avec les autorités, la principale force d’opposition au Pakistan a commencé, dimanche 4 octobre, une grande marche en soutien à l’ancien Premier ministre Imran Khan, incarcéré depuis 2023, pour accroître la pression sur le gouvernement. Mais les autorités, qui considèrent l’ancien Premier ministre comme une menace pour la sécurité nationale, ont interdit toute manifestation dans la capitale, Islamabad. Elles y ont déployé des moyens colossaux pour empêcher les manifestants d’entrer.

Canada: jour de vote au Québec, avec les souverainistes en favoris dans un scrutin qui s'annonce indécis. Au Québec, c’est jour de vote ce lundi 5 octobre. Après 39 jours de campagne dominée par le coût de la vie, la santé et l’avenir politique de la province, une même envie domine toujours : celle du changement. L’usure du pouvoir sortant a rouvert le jeu avec les indépendantistes en tête des sondages. Cinq forces peuvent peser dans les urnes sans qu'une majorité ne se dégage dans les sondages. Une fragmentation politique que le Québec n’avait plus connue depuis près d’un demi-siècle.

Crise du logement en Espagne: Pedro Sanchez convoque des élections anticipées le 29 novembre. Le Premier ministre espagnol Pedro Sanchez a annoncé, lundi 5 octobre, qu'il allait convoquer des élections législatives anticipées le 29 novembre prochain, après le rejet vendredi des mesures que son gouvernement avait présentées pour tenter de sortir l'Espagne de la crise du logement.

En pleine tempête canado-américaine, la question de l'indépendance refait surface au Québec. On vote aujourd'hui pour les élections provinciales au Québec, la province francophone du Canada. Dans un contexte de relations tendues entre le Canada et les États-Unis, et où le Premier ministre Mark Carney incarne la résistance face à Donald Trump, la question de l'organisation d'un nouveau référendum sur l'indépendance a été remise sur la table.

Cesaria Evora: «Reina da Morna», l’album inédit, quinze ans après sa mort. Quinze ans après la mort de Cesaria Evora, dix chansons inédites enregistrées au fil de sa carrière paraissent sur Reina da Morna. José Da Silva, son producteur et manager historique, revient sur l’histoire de ces titres, mais aussi la personnalité de la star capverdienne.

Royaume-Uni: ouverture du procès de 12 accusés dans une version britannique de l'affaire Pelicot. Au Royaume-Uni s’ouvre ce lundi le procès des coaccusés de l’affaire « Pelicot britannique ». Un homme d'une soixantaine d'années a plaidé coupable d’avoir drogué et violé son épouse pendant plus de vingt ans dans une affaire aux nombreuses similitudes avec celle des viols de Mazan.

Climat : une pré-COP31 inédite dans le Pacifique, l'Australie attendue au tournant. Quelques semaines avant la COP 31, qui se tiendra en Turquie, Fidji et Tuvalu accueillent du 5 au 8 octobre une pré-COP, la première de l’histoire, destinée à mettre l’accent sur les difficultés pour les nations insulaires, les plus directement menacées par le réchauffement climatique. L’Australie, qui co-accueille la prochaine COP avec la Turquie, aura le rôle de négociateur en chef et envisage de se faire un porte-voix puissant de ce qu’elle désigne comme sa « famille du Pacifique ». Mais les relations entre ces pays et leur voisin australien sont très ambivalentes.

Romuald Sciora: «Trump se prépare à contester les résultats des élections de mi-mandat». Romuald Sciora, directeur de l'observatoire politique et géostratégique des États-Unis de l'Iris et auteur de Lettre ouverte à Trump d'un Américain de papier (Ed. Point Nemo) est ce lundi 5 octobre le grand invité international de la matinale de RFI. À un mois des élections de mi-mandat aux États-Unis, les sondages prédisent une défaite du camp présidentiel. Selon Romuald Sciora, on ne peut exclure l'hypothèse d'une tentative de coup de force de la part du président américain.

Washington rapatrie ses bombardiers déployés dans une base anglaise sur fond de menace d'attaque iranienne. Les États-Unis ont retiré leurs bombardiers stratégiques B-1 de la base aérienne britannique de Fairford, à la suite, selon des médias américains, de nouvelles menaces visant ce site militaire. Celui-ci est au cœur d’une enquête antiterroriste aux multiples zones d’ombre.

Le prix Nobel de médecine est décerné à Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann et Georg Nagel. Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann et Georg Nagel sont récompensés « pour leurs découvertes concernant les canaux ioniques photosensibles et l'optogénétique », une méthode qui permet de montrer comment les cellules nerveuses façonnent les souvenirs, les émotions et les comportements dans le cerveau. Karl Deisseroth est de nationalité américaine, Peter Hegemann et Georg Nagel, allemande.

Yémen: la coalition dirigée par Riyad dit rejoindre l'offensive du gouvernement contre les Houthis. La coalition militaire dirigée par Riyad a annoncé lundi rejoindre l’offensive lancée la veille par le gouvernement yéménite contre les combattants pro-iraniens houthis, en mobilisant 100 avions de combat pour mener des frappes à l’aube.

États-Unis: une Chinoise arrêtée à Los Angeles, accusée de surveiller la famille du président taïwanais. Le FBI a appréhendé une agente immobilière de 34 ans, soupçonnée d'espionner la famille du président taïwanais, à l'aéroport de Los Angeles alors qu'elle tentait de rentrer en Chine ce dimanche 4 octobre. Une affaire rapidement dénoncée par Taipei comme une forme de « répression transnationale ». Selon les autorités américaines, elle faisait remonter à des agents chinois des informations sur les déplacements du fils de Lai Ching-te.

Immeuble, vols et avion privé, l'extrême droite australienne gâtée par la femme la plus riche du pays. En Australie, le parti d’extrême droite One Nation réalise une forte percée dans les sondages depuis fin 2026 et l’attentat de Bondi. Pour surfer sur sa popularité, la formation politique peut compter sur le soutien financier de la plus grosse fortune du pays, Gina Rinehart, une héritière très proche de Donald Trump et d’Elon Musk, à la tête d’un empire minier. Dernier cadeau en date, un immeuble situé proche du centre de Brisbane, où le parti compte installer son quartier général…

Mali: l'armée en mouvement dans la région de Kidal. Au Mali, d'importants convois de l'armée sont arrivés à Anéfis et Aguelhoc pendant le week-end. Il s'agit des deux derniers camps contrôlés par l'armée dans la région de Kidal, depuis que les indépendantistes du FLA et les jihadistes du Jnim, liés à al-Qaïda, se sont emparés de Kidal et Tessalit en avril dernier. Le 4 octobre au soir et le 5 octobre au matin, des frappes aériennes ont été effectuées dans la région. L'armée n'a pas dévoilé ses intentions, mais ces mouvements pourraient préfigurer un début d'opération de reconquête.

Expulsé des États-Unis puis détenu en Eswatini, un migrant libéré témoigne avant de rejoindre le Laos. Il avait été expulsé des États-Unis, où il a passé l’essentiel de sa vie, vers l’Eswatini, la dernière monarchie absolue d’Afrique. Après 15 mois dans une prison de haute sécurité dans ce pays, Phone Chomsavanh vient d’être libéré. Il est l’un des visages de la politique d’expulsions de Donald Trump vers des pays tiers, dénoncée par l’ONU comme contraire au droit international. Ce Laotien est désormais en route vers le Laos, son pays de nationalité qu’il connaît pourtant à peine. Un soulagement, donc, mais aussi beaucoup d’incertitudes pour cet homme qui a grandi aux États-Unis.

«L'union de la gauche est un impératif», alerte la députée écologiste Cyrielle Chatelain. Cyrielle Chatelain, députée de l'Isère et présidente du groupe Écologiste et social à l'Assemblée nationale, l'assure : le budget 2027 « ne répond en rien à toutes les urgences du moment » – qu'elles soient sociales ou écologiques – en plus d'être « incompatible avec toute volonté d'améliorer les conditions des services publics ». Face à l'extrême droite, la députée, unioniste de la première heure, défend aussi l'alliance de la gauche pour faire réellement avancer l'écologie, « sinon, nous risquons 5 ans de recul écologiste extrêmement violent », alerte-t-elle.

Death of girl, 11, being treated as 'unexplained' after body found in park. Police are treating the death of an 11-year-old girl as "unexplained" after her body was found in a park in Worcestershire.
Cleverly hits out at Braverman over 'Englishness' row. Sir James Cleverly has criticised former Conservative colleague Suella Braverman after she sparked a row around "Englishness".

US 'closely monitoring' after Russian lab worker 'dies of suspected plague'. Marco Rubio has said the US is "closely monitoring" the case involving the death of a laboratory worker in Russia who may have been exposed to pneumonic plague.

'Hundreds of Houthi targets in Yemen attacked' in air campaign by Saudi-led coalition. A Saudi-led coalition says it has attacked 324 "high-value targets" in an operation involving 100 fighter jets against the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen.

Sainsbury's held talks about merger with supermarket rival Morrisons. J Sainsbury held merger talks with rival grocer Morrisons earlier this year - a deal that would have represented the most significant tie-up in the sector for more than five years.
Failed asylum seeker who attempted knife attack on Israeli embassy jailed for life. A failed asylum seeker who tried to launch a knife attack on London's Israeli embassy has been jailed for life.

Removal of US bombers from RAF Fairford not directly tied to arrests, says Rubio. The removal of US bombers from RAF Fairford is not directly connected to the arrests of five men near the base, the US secretary of state has said.
Murder investigation launched after body found in burning van. A murder investigation has been launched after a body was found inside a burning van.

The question you would ask HPE and NVIDIA if nobody was recording. The Register’s data sovereignty dinner in Washington puts HPE’s and NVIDIA’s AI infrastructure leads at one table, off the record, on 29 October.

Die Rückkehr der Judenverfolgung. Was in den drei mächtigsten Ländern Europas passiert, stellt einen Zivilisationsbruch dar: Die Linke in Deutschland, Frankreich und Großbritannien umarmt den Antisemitismus.

Wenn sich arabische Jugendliche „entfalten“. Am Rande der Einheits-Feier in Bremen wurden zwei Homosexuelle von jungen Arabern zusammengeschlagen. Solche Fälle häufen sich. Aber in Deutschland kämpft man lieber gegen „Islamophobie“.

„Unangebracht und falsch“ – Wadephul kritisiert SPD-Politiker wegen Aussage zu Flydubai-Anschlag. Ein Posting des Menschenrechtsbeauftragten Castellucci zum versuchten Anschlag auf einen Flydubai-Flug sorgt weiter für Kritik. Nun äußert sich Außenminister Wadephul.

Was Merz den Deutschen nicht sagt. Die Milliarden-Hilfen für die Ukraine werden in Deutschland unpopulärer. Der Kanzler verteidigt sie dennoch – doch er verschweigt einen entscheidenden Grund für seinen Kurs.

„Hochgradig irritiert“ – Günther warnt Kanzler in Brief vor Reiches Energiepolitik. Schleswig-Holsteins Ministerpräsident Günther fordert eine Kurskorrektur bei mehreren Vorhaben von Wirtschaftsministerin Reiche (CDU). Diese könnten Deutschland und seinem Bundesland schaden.

„Eine ehrliche Veränderung der Position der Linkspartei wird unterbleiben“. Frank Steffel (CDU) appelliert an die Berliner Sozialdemokraten, sich bei ihren Verhandlungen mit der Linkspartei „ihrer historischen Verantwortung bewusst“ zu werden: „Aber ich gehe davon aus, dass es in der SPD in Berlin eine Mehrheit für Gespräche gibt.“

Zweiter Gardasee unter Venedig? Forscher machen spektakuläre Entdeckung. Tief unter der Küste bei Venedig haben Forscher ein gewaltiges Süßwasservorkommen entdeckt. Die verborgene Reserve könnte helfen, ein regionales Problem langfristig zu lösen.

„In der Ukraine gibt es eine große Sorge, dass die deutsche Unterstützung nachlassen könnte“. In der Ukraine blickt man mit Sorge auf die Ergebnisse der Landtagswahlen in Sachsen-Anhalt, MeckPomm und Berlin. „Die Sorge ist hier groß, dass man keine Unterstützung mehr bekommen könnte“, so Axel Springer Global Reporter Paul Ronzheimer.

„Wir kamen kaum über 20 km/h hinaus. Es ist beängstigend, so etwas zu sehen“. In Malaysia kommt es zum Image-Crash für die Formel 1. Mehrere Autos rollen nur noch über die Strecke. Es sei wie bei einem „Lego-Rennen“ gewesen, sagt Sieger Verstappen. Nun bedarf es schnellster Aufklärung – sonst droht eine Wiederholung.

Mann greift Zugbegleiterin an – und wird überwältigt und gefesselt. Eskalation in einem Zug von Halle nach Erfurt: Ein Fahrgast geht bei der Ticketkontrolle auf die Zugbegleiterin los. Sicherheitsleute können den Mann fassen, später nahm ihn die Polizei fest.

„Extremismus wird nicht harmloser, wenn er aus dem eigenen politischen Lager kommt“. Autor Hasnain Kazim kritisiert den unterschiedlichen Umgang mit Wahlsiegen von AfD und Linkspartei. Zudem warnt er davor, Verfassungsschutz-Einstufungen bei Linksextremismus und der Organisation Rote Hilfe zu verharmlosen.

Neuwahlen in Spanien – und Premier Sánchez bleibt nur eine einzige Hoffnung. Toilet seats, toys and hair clips: The strangest items Israel still barred from Gaza Submitted by Maha Hussaini on Fri, 10/02/2026 - 10:51 A year after the ceasefire, Palestinians still struggle to find everyday items as restrictions keep basic and non-essential goods off the market Palestinians go about their daily lives amid rainfall in Gaza City on 1 October 2026 (Mohammed M Skaik/JNA Press via Reuters) Off A toilet seat is all that stands between Dima Awad and moving out of her makeshift tent before winter. The 48-year-old Palestinian mother has rented a small garage in western Gaza City and has already moved most of her belongings there. But she cannot move in until she finds a toilet seat, something that has become increasingly difficult to find in Gaza. The basic item is among a range of essential goods that Israel continues to prevent from entering the besieged enclave. “I paid the rent around 10 days ago, and I’ve been looking for a proper toilet at an affordable price for about two weeks now,” said Awad, who now lives with her only son after being separated from her husband, who travelled for treatment during the genocide . (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); “Of course, there is no way to find a new toilet seat at an affordable price right now. The second-hand ones are also unsuitable and still expensive.” Due to their scarcity, toilet seats in Gaza now cost between 1,500 and 2,000 shekels ($486-648). “I have done everything possible to move from my tent so that we wouldn’t get soaked by rainwater like we did last year. But the garage I found doesn’t have a toilet, so we have to build our own,” Awad told Middle East Eye. “I consider the garage rent affordable after all the other unaffordable apartments I tried to rent. It costs around 600 shekels ($194) a month. But now I have to find a toilet that costs twice as much as the rent.” A ghost list of barred items Following the imposition of its blockade on the Gaza Strip in 2007, Israel barred or restricted the entry of numerous items, classifying them as “ dual-use ” goods that could potentially be used for military purposes. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); These included construction materials, water and sewage pumps, electrical equipment, generators, medical equipment, wheelchairs, crutches and other items needed for basic civilian life. In the first two years of the genocide that began in October 2023, Israel sealed Gaza’s crossings and severely restricted the entry of commercial goods and humanitarian aid, including food, medicine, fuel and other essential supplies. Under the October 2025 ceasefire agreement, Israel was required to lift its restrictions and facilitate the flow of international humanitarian aid into Gaza. 'We are being left without either the essentials or the non-essentials' - Imad Sersawi, Palestinian father Yet, nearly a year later, vast restrictions remain, including on medicine, shelter, reconstruction materials, and other essential and non-essential items. A range of everyday civilian and humanitarian items continue to be denied entry under what aid workers have described as a “ghost list”. The restrictions do not stop at goods with obvious humanitarian or reconstruction uses. They extend to seemingly mundane everyday items such as batteries, lighters and children’s toys. “I have a lighter that the entire camp borrows whenever they need to light a fire for cooking,” said Imad Sersawi, a 45-year-old Palestinian displaced from the Shujaiya neighbourhood. “Today, whoever has a lighter is considered rich because a single lighter costs 90 shekels ($29),” he added. “You wouldn’t even find it easily in the markets because they haven’t been allowed in months.” Disappearing items The father of five said more and more items are disappearing from Gaza’s markets, making everyday life increasingly uncertain. “One day you find something; the next day it’s banned and disappears for God knows how long. Some things haven’t been allowed in for years,” he said. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); “For example, I haven’t bought any toys for my children since the beginning of the genocide. Before the ceasefire agreement, they used to cry and ask for toys, and I would scold them for not understanding the situation and asking for unavailable things,” he explained. “I used to tell them that once the war was over, I would buy them toys.” One year after Gaza ceasefire, killing and displacement of Palestinians persist Read More » But even after the ceasefire agreement, Israel continued to bar toys from entering Gaza. Today, toy shops are selling whatever remains from before the war at exorbitant prices. “I cannot buy them a small rubber ball for 100 shekels [$32]. That amount would feed the entire family for two days,” Sersawi continued. “People outside Gaza might say that basic necessities are missing and that we are focusing on these secondary things. But the fact is that we are being left without either the essentials or the non-essentials.” The system governing these restrictions remains opaque. Israel has not published a comprehensive, updated list of dual-use items since 2017, while hundreds of items have been added to the restrictions without being publicly listed. In practice, aid organisations and traders have had to navigate a system in which goods can be rejected because they fall outside the humanitarian category or are deemed “dual-use”. ‘Making the simplest things a struggle’ Everyday objects that would normally be taken for granted have also become difficult to find. Baidaa Othman, a Palestinian journalist, had to travel between two governorates to find a hair claw clip, eventually paying around 10 times its original price. “Now it’s not just about being able to get the basic necessities. It has reached a point where, when you want to buy something very simple, you have to go to extraordinary lengths to find it,” Othman told MEE. “Even the simplest things as basic as a hair clip have become difficult to find. On top of all the basic necessities that are unavailable in Gaza, now the everyday things that no one would normally think twice about have become unavailable.” In an Instagram video , Sojood Hasan, a Palestinian physiotherapist in Gaza, highlighted how restrictions on hair clips reflect a wider loss of everyday choices for women in the Strip. “No one collapses because a hair clip is missing. But the feeling that your life is not in your hands can wear you down,” the young woman said. 'This is not random; it is a policy of making even the simplest things a struggle for Gazans' - Baidaa Othman, Palestinian journalist For Othman, who is originally from Gaza City and remains displaced in Deir al-Balah in central Gaza after her home was destroyed, the need for such an ordinary item is inseparable from the daily realities of displacement. “On top of the displacement and all the hardships we face, including having to cook with firewood, it’s only natural for women to want to put their hair up to keep it off their faces and necks in the heat. So it’s not a secondary item any more,” she said. A clip that once cost around four shekels ($1.3) cost her 45 shekels ($14.5). “The Israeli occupation knows exactly what it is doing,” Othman said. “This is not random; it is a policy of making even the simplest things a struggle for Gazans.” Israel's genocide in Gaza Gaza City, occupied Palestine News Post Date Override 0 Update Date Mon, 05/04/2020 - 21:19 Update Date Override 0

Is Ethiopia repeating its oldest mistake? Submitted by Yunus Turhan on Thu, 10/01/2026 - 16:33 When past leaders have tried to govern from a single centre, the country's peripheries have united in opposition Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed attends a meeting in Moscow on 25 September 2025 (Evgenia Novozhenina/AFP) On Ethiopia’s history has come back to haunt it. Late last month, seven armed groups - among them the Fano militia in Amhara, the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) and the Oromo Liberation Army - announced the formation of the Ethiopian Peoples’ Forces Alliance for Survival, and vowed to remove Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed. Within days, Tigrayan forces had seized the airports in Mekelle, Axum and Shire, and opened fronts in Afar and Amhara. By 25 September, phone and internet lines in Tigray were cut . This time it was the TPLF, not Addis Ababa, that ordered the blackout. Most commentary reads the new conflict as the collapse of the Pretoria agreement , a 2022 peace deal to end two years of war. But the story is much older than the Pretoria process and Abiy himself. For nearly two centuries, Ethiopian politics has swung between a centre that wants to command, and regions that insist on ruling themselves. Each time the pendulum has pushed hard towards the centre, the peripheries have found a way to unite against it. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); After the Zemane Mesafint (“ Era of the Princes ”) in the 18th and 19th centuries, when regional lords ran their own affairs, Tewodros II tried to rebuild the empire by the sword. The provinces revolted one after another, and in 1868, he died at Magdala, his army reduced to remnants. Similarly, former emperor Haile Selassie’s 1962 dissolution of the Eritrean federation turned a small insurgency into a 30-year war. The Derg regime pushed centralisation to its limits, and fell in 1991 to a coalition of ethno-regional groups, the Ethiopian People’s Revolutionary Democratic Front (EPRDF). The 1995 constitution swung back by creating ethnic federalism and, in Article 39, even a right to secession. Yet the EPRDF ran that system through party discipline from Addis Ababa, so self-rule stayed largely on paper. In short, Ethiopia’s state structure has swung between centralisation and decentralisation over 170 years. Tensions unresolved Abiy assumed power in 2018 by preaching Medemer , an approach of reconciliation and national unity in the face of ethnic divisions. But it quickly began to unravel in 2019, when he dissolved the EPRDF to form his Prosperity Party. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Tensions long kept under wraps soon boiled over, and to contain them, Abiy returned to the tools of his predecessors: mass arrests of suspected opponents, and new restrictions on the media. War with the TPLF followed in 2020 , fought alongside forces from Eritrea and Amhara. After the Pretoria agreement in 2022, Abiy disbanded the regional special forces, which pushed the Fano militia into open revolt. The status of Welkait and Raya , claimed by both Amhara and Tigray, was left unresolved after Pretoria, so both sides felt cheated. The coalition now marching against Abiy is largely made up of the forces with which he won the last war What made such an unlikely alliance possible? The answer lies less with the rebels than with the centre’s own choices. Each centralising step cost Abiy a partner. Eritrea, kept away from the Pretoria negotiating table, watched its old enemy survive, and then heard Addis Ababa speak of a Red Sea port in terms Asmara read as a claim on Assab . The special forces decision did the same to Amhara. In short, the coalition now marching against Abiy is largely made up of the forces with which he won the last war. Can the new alliance muster the capacity to challenge Abiy’s rule? This is not likely, at least for the time being. The alliance has named no joint military commander, and unlike 1991, it has no dominant force able to march on the capital. Abiy has a drone fleet the Derg never had, along with a fresh mandate from the public, as his party won 438 of the 501 contested seats in parliament (nearly 90 percent) this past June. But some groups have rejected the results, and voting did not take place in Tigray, which comprises 38 constituencies. The road ahead Three paths seem possible from here for Abiy. In the first, he peels Amhara away with concessions over Welkait, while the TPLF’s seizure of airports enables him to present it as the aggressor. The price is that any Welkait deal with Fano locks Tigray into permanent war, so dividing the alliance on one front deepens the other. In the second, the war settles into a stalemate: the centre holds the cities and the skies, armed movements hold the countryside, and Ethiopia drifts towards a de facto confederation run by men with guns - a Zemene Mesafint by other means. The third is the most dangerous. Abiy has a record of seeking a unifying cause abroad when pressed at home; once it was the Renaissance Dam (where Egypt is a factor), and today it is access to the sea. This time, a move towards Assab would turn a civil war into a war with Eritrea, and pull in every regional power watching. The regional map explains why that third path cannot be dismissed. The fault lines of Sudan ’s war now run through Ethiopia. On one side sits the UAE , Abiy’s main supporter since 2018, whose drones are widely credited with turning the last war, and which analysts accuse of routing arms through Ethiopia to Sudan’s Rapid Support Forces . Gold, arms and mercenaries: On UAE's shadowy networks in Sudan Read More » Israel ’s recognition of Somaliland in December 2025, widely seen as brokered by Abu Dhabi, and President Isaac Herzog’s visit to Addis Ababa in February tied Ethiopia’s hunger for the sea to Emirati-Israeli designs for the Red Sea. On the other side, Egypt, which regards the Renaissance Dam as a threat to its survival, has built an axis with Eritrea and Somalia , and backs Sudan’s army , with Saudi Arabia reportedly drawing closer to Asmara. A simultaneous rift with Egypt and Eritrea would carry a heavy price for Abiy Ahmed's government, since Addis Ababa would then face hostile fault lines to both its north and its east. Cairo has pledged troops to the African Union mission in Somalia, and Eritrea has already placed itself at the heart of the dispute by severing diplomatic relations with Ethiopia altogether. Hemmed in on both flanks, Ethiopia would depend almost entirely on Djibouti, which already handles close to 90 percent of its trade . For Ahmed, a war on several fronts would revive what Otto von Bismarck called his "cauchemar des coalitions", the "nightmare of coalitions" in which France and Russia might join forces and drag Germany into a two-front war. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Fighting at home while quarrelling abroad would be the worst of all scenarios for Addis Ababa, once the military costs, the strain on debt relief and the human toll are counted together. For Cairo, an Ethiopia tied down at home is leverage on the Nile. For Abu Dhabi, a collapsing Ethiopia would mean losing its most valuable partner on the mainland. Both camps thus have reasons to feed the war, yet neither has much interest in a clear winner. That is how civil wars become proxy wars. This is where Turkey matters. It brokered the Ankara Declaration between Ethiopia and Somalia in December 2024, while holding its largest overseas base in Mogadishu, and has mended ties with both Cairo and Abu Dhabi in recent years. This gives Ankara a rare ability to speak to both camps. As his room at home narrows, Abiy may well knock on Ankara’s door again. Ethiopia’s prognosis therefore hinges on Abiy’s next move: whether he adopts collaborative, win-win strategies towards his opponents, or clings to a zero-sum game. In making that choice, he would do well to look back, for Ethiopian history is clear on one point: the state has held when power was bargained with the regions, and it has cracked whenever power was imposed on them. The reason is simple. Once power has been devolved to the peripheries, it can rarely be recentralised without resistance - and this is precisely the lesson Abiy must now come to terms with. Israel bans Zack Polanski after Green Party backs 'Zionism is racism' motion Submitted by MEE staff on Mon, 10/05/2026 - 10:04 Israel's foreign ministry accuses Green Party of legitimising 'destruction of the state of Israel' Zack Polanski (right), poses for a photo in London on 12 September, ahead of the Holborn and St Pancras by-election (AFP/Toby Shepheard) Off Israel has banned Green Party leader Zack Polanski from entering the country after the party approved a motion at its conference declaring "Zionism is racism". In a statement on Sunday, Israel accused the Green Party of England and Wales of legitimising "the destruction of the State of Israel". Israel’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said the resolution, which also advocates for a one-state solution in historic Palestine , “constitutes a clear antisemitic text according to the IHRA definition, as it denies the Jewish people’s right to self-determination”. “Therefore, as a first step, foreign minister Gideon Sa’ar has decided this evening to declare Green Party leader Zack Polanski barred from entering Israel,” it said. According to Israel's Law of Return, persons with at least one Jewish grandparent, and their spouses, have a legal right to enter, reside in, and acquire citizenship of, the State of Israel. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); However, Israel has occasionally banned certain Jewish people from entering the country if it deems them a security risk, or they question Israel's legitimacy. In practice, this has often meant political opponents of the state. The vote by party members on Sunday makes the Green Party the first major party in the UK to recognise Zionism as a form of racism - and to back a single democratic Palestinian state with equal rights for all ethnic and religious groups, rather than a two-state solution. At the conference in Brighton this weekend, 1,022 members voted for the motion while 813 voted against it. Co-deputy leader Mothin Ali told Middle East Eye on Sunday that he was strongly in favour of the motion, unlike Green MPs Carla Denyer and Adrian Ramsay, who criticised it. 'We're waiting to sweep up their votes': Three days inside the Green Party conference Read More » "As defined in the motion," Ali said, "Zionism is an ethno-nationalist state. Zionism is resulting in ethnic cleansing, in the belief that one group of people is superior to another." Green members voted against an amendment to the motion saying it "shall not be used to pressure, proscribe or discipline members based on affiliation with Jewish community institutions, such as synagogues, community centres or denominational groups, that describe themselves as Zionist or used to discipline or sanction Jewish members for expressing views that would be non sanctionable if expressed by non Jewish members (such as support for a binational state, or two state solution)." But members voted for an amendment supporting the "inalienable right to self-determination" for Palestinians, party insiders told MEE. Party spokespeople on Sunday morning would not say whether Polanski would support the motion without amendments. After the vote, the five Green MPs published a joint statement saying: "We will never tolerate any form of discrimination or harassment". They added that "there is no conflict between supporting the rights of Palestinians and the rights of Jewish people." Three years after Israeli bombing, Palestinian man recovers wife's remains Submitted by Ahmed Dremly on Mon, 10/05/2026 - 10:08 Adham Heriz spent years searching for his family beneath the ruins of their Gaza City home. A new civil defence operation recovered the remains of 105 Palestinians, but his son is still missing A mass funeral for 105 Palestinians whose remains were recovered from beneath the rubble of destroyed buildings in the al-Taj area of Gaza City's al-Yarmouk neighbourhood, 1 October 2026 (Bilal Osama/Apaimages via Reuters) Off For nearly three years, Adham Heriz, 41, waited to recover and bury the bodies of his wife and children. On Thursday, after years of searching through the ruins of their neighbourhood in eastern Gaza City, the Palestinian father finally recovered the remains of his wife, Hiam, 37. His son’s body is still missing. Hiam and their eldest son, Anas, 17, were killed when a heavy Israeli bombardment completely destroyed their home in Al-Yarmouk on 25 October 2023. According to the Palestinian civil defence spokesperson in Gaza, Mahmoud Basal, the attack involved a series of heavy Israeli bombardments that struck 18 buildings containing around 175 residential apartments. Around 450 people were inside the buildings, including doctors, academics, journalists, children and infants, Basal told MEE. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); “There were people thrown by the explosion around 200 metres. Entire families were wiped out. Many dead bodies were completely disintegrated, leaving little or no trace behind because of the massive explosives used in the bombs,” he said. At the time, civil defence teams were able to recover only 120 bodies because Israeli forces were advancing and continuing to attack the area. Much of the heavy equipment and vehicles needed to move the rubble had also been destroyed. Hiam’s remains were among those of 105 people recovered from beneath the rubble during a 20-day civil defence operation in the neighbourhood last week. “I found the remains of my wife and my brother and his family, but I did not find the body of my son,” Heriz told Middle East Eye. A black cloud Heriz and his family of seven lived on the sixth floor of a seven-storey building. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); On 25 October, they had lunch together. Hiam and two of their daughters went to the kitchen to wash the dishes. Minutes later, Israeli strikes hit the area. “It was like a black cloud covering everything,” Heriz recalled. Gaza siblings pulled from rubble left reeling after pregnant mother’s death Read More » “I felt like I was flying and being thrown under the rubble with each strike. I could not hear anything. I could not breathe because of the bomb powder and dust. “I was thinking about my family. I managed to pull myself out from under the rubble. I saw my son Ahmed, eight, alive but bleeding heavily beside me, before I collapsed because most of my bones were broken.” His two youngest daughters, Siwar, three, and Dima, 10, also escaped the rubble, both seriously wounded. Ahmed survived the attack. But Hiam, Anas and their two elder daughters, Shahad, 18, and Dareen, 15, were killed and remained beneath the rubble. Heriz’s brother and his family of five were also killed. “People moved me to an ambulance while I was crying for my family under the rubble. ‘Forgive me, my children. I can't pull you out. I can't feel my hands; they are broken,’” he said. With the help of civil defence search-and-rescue workers and residents, the bodies of Heriz’s daughters, Shahad and Dareen, were recovered. Voices beneath the rubble But rescuers could not move the vast amount of rubble needed to reach Hiam, Anas and others believed to be trapped beneath the destroyed building. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Heriz and his relatives repeatedly searched the site, but without the equipment needed to clear the debris, they were unable to recover the remaining bodies. 'We found a less-than-one-year-old child in his crib beneath the rubble, still holding his milk pacifier in his hand' - Adham Heriz, Palestinian father He had lost hope of finding his family’s remains until civil defence teams began a new operation in the area last month. The operation was coordinated with the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), with vehicles supplied by Egypt and fuel provided through Ocha, the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs. “During the 20-day search, we were able to pull up the bodies of 37 dead children alone from under the building I was living in,” Heriz said. “We found a less-than-one-year-old child in his crib beneath the rubble, still holding his milk pacifier in his hand. When his father saw him and identified him by the clothes he was wearing, he collapsed from the shock.” As the operation continued, Heriz finally found the remains of his wife, his brother and his brother’s family. But his son’s body was not found. Andrew Feinstein: The anti-apartheid activist trying to stop Keir Starmer Read More » “The man who helped break the region is now selling himself as the one to fix it – for a fee.” Making a Killing lays bare how executives and politicians arranged a price for human lives in corporate boardrooms, never having to face the cost of their actions halfway across the world. It is unlikely to amount to straightforward disarmament, instead seeking to limit these groups’ ability to act autonomously by bringing their weapons more closely under state control and, in some cases, integrating fighters into formal state structures. Iraq’s Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi has now set a deadline of 30 June 2027 to complete this process. Whether the process succeeds will depend on Baghdad’s ability to manage the demands of armed groups, their willingness to accept limits on their autonomy and, crucially, whether external actors avoid actions that could undermine it. In recent weeks, a framework for enforcing state control over Iraq’s paramilitary groups has emerged. According to Zaidi, Baghdad plans to implement the process in phases, starting with a 90-day cessation of military activity. This period began on 30 September, on the same day the US-led coalition, which has for years come under attacks by these groups, officially withdrew from Iraq. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); In return, the US would refrain from launching military strikes on armed groups in Iraq. During the United States' war on Iran , the US military repeatedly struck bases affiliated with Iran-linked paramilitaries, including the Popular Mobilisation Forces (PMF). On 29 July, Saudi Arabia and the US launched a joint attack on PMF targets, killing at least 20 members. Following the three-month period, paramilitary groups, many of which formerly operated under the PMF and are already embedded within the state, will begin the process of bringing their weapons under state control. What this means in practice remains unclear. According to a statement made on 2 September by Nouri al-Maliki, leader of the State of Law Coalition and a former Iraqi prime minister, the process is not disarmament in the traditional sense, but the containment and control of weapons by the state. Iran-linked armed groups in Iraq have over the years launched rocket attacks, one-way attack drone and long-range missile attacks on US interests in Iraq and the wider region, and reportedly against energy and other strategic infrastructure in the Gulf. The process also aims to limit these groups’ ability to undertake unilateral military action beyond Iraq’s borders, reducing the risk of Iraq being drawn into regional escalation. Actions by these groups, including drone strikes on Israel during the war in Gaza and attacks on US interests during the war on Iran, have previously risked doing just that. Baghdad also appears to be seeking to integrate fighters from some paramiltaries operating outside the PMF into its ranks as individuals, rather than preserving their existing command structures. Without naming the groups involved, Zaidi said in an interview in late September that his goal was “to end the existence of these factions as independent entities”. For many of these groups, however, accepting a proposal that limits their ability to launch military attacks and operate autonomously would require guarantees that Baghdad would be willing to protect their interests. Meeting demands Iraq’s array of paramilitary groups, with varying degrees of proximity to Iran, wield different levels of political and economic influence. These dynamics are likely to shape the bargaining process between the groups and Baghdad. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Some groups, such as Asaib Ahl al-Haq (AAH) and Kataeb Imam Ali, announced in June that they would place their arms under state control. For AAH, however, continued willingness to do so is likely contingent on its ability to preserve its economic influence and the parliamentary seats held by its affiliated Sadiqoon bloc. At the time, more hardline factions such as Harakat Hezbollah al-Nujaba and Kataeb Hezbollah – which, under the banner of the Islamic Resistance of Iraq (IRI), participated in recent attacks on US interests in the region – refused to disarm. These groups have cited the continued US presence in Iraq, among other factors, as a reason for retaining their weapons. However, in late August, these groups announced conditions for placing their weapons under state control. On the day of the US-led coalition’s withdrawal from Iraq, Kataeb Hezbollah said it would halt all military activity except against hostile aircraft. The move broadly aligns with Zaidi’s efforts to de-escalate tensions before bringing these groups under tighter state control. Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi delivers a speech during the Sovereignty Day Conference marking the withdrawal of US-led coalition forces from Iraq, in Baghdad, on 1 October 2026 (Iraqi Prime Minister's Media Office/HO/Reuters) (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); There has been progress on some of the key demands put forward by these groups. On 1 October, Ankara announced that the Bashiqa-Zelikan military camp near Mosul would be handed to the Iraqi government under an agreed mechanism and timetable, meeting a key demand of paramilitary groups for the withdrawal of Turkish troops from northern Iraq. In parallel, efforts are underway to remove the Kurdistan Workers’ Party (PKK) from the area, another demand made by the groups. Still, Baghdad may find it difficult to meet all of their demands. In August, the Islamic Resistance in Iraq called for the “liberation” of Iraq’s political and economic decision-making from US “hegemony”. Paramilitary groups affiliated with the IRI have previously cited US control over Iraq’s oil revenues as an example. Since 2003, Iraq’s oil revenues have been held at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York and transferred to Iraq monthly in US dollars. Notably, groups including Kataeb Hezbollah, Kataeb Sayyid al-Shuhada, Harakat al-Nujaba and Ansar Allah al-Awfiya have in recent months called for strengthening Iraq’s air defences and preventing foreign aircraft from using Iraqi airspace to strike neighbouring countries, including Iran. Any renewed US strikes on Iran, particularly during the 90-day period, could therefore undermine efforts to integrate some Iraqi armed groups and increase the risk of clashes between these groups and Baghdad. A balancing act Iraq’s prime minister can bring paramilitary weapons under state control only if he can balance the interests of these groups with those of Washington. The extent of state control, how far the state will go in dismantling autonomous command structures, and where these groups will fit within Iraq’s state structures remain subject to debate. The implementation of the plan will therefore depend on whether all key parties are willing to avoid maximalist positions that could stall the process. “Washington has not expressed an opposing stance to Zaidi’s current proposal, or to the militia’s demands. But clarity around Washington’s red lines are required for the process to move forward,” Mustafa al-Saray, director of research at the Bayan Centre for Strategic Studies, an Iraq-based think tank, told Middle East Eye. With US troops departing, Iraq looks beyond balancing Washington and Tehran Read More » “Similarly, even though most of these militias appear receptive to Zaidi’s plan, there is always a chance that Tehran objects to the process, and this would also change the negotiation process in Iraq.” Iran-linked groups in Iraq have already demonstrated their readiness to challenge decisions made by Baghdad. On 25 September, Iraq suspended all flights to Iran after the US announced sweeping secondary sanctions on the Iranian aviation industry. But after a Kataeb Hezbollah security official warned that Zaidi’s government could be “brought down”, Washington granted a one-month sanctions waiver allowing Iraqi Airways to operate flights between Iran and the Shia holy city of Najaf. Still, if Zaidi fails to manage competing interests in Baghdad and Washington, Iraqi paramilitary groups could turn against the new prime minister, who came to power in May after the US effectively vetoed their preferred candidate. “There is a real risk that Iraq returns to the pre-2022 equation, where the militias held prime ministers directly responsible for international actions against them,” said Saray. Renewed and sustained US strikes on Iran would also likely undermine prospects for a peaceful integration process. As seen during the previous escalation, Baghdad would likely struggle to prevent some Iraqi armed groups from launching attacks in support of Iran, potentially derailing the current de-escalation. Moreover, like after the US-Saudi strikes on the PMF in late July, further foreign attacks on Iraq’s paramilitaries would almost certainly harden their stance against accepting greater state oversight. His brilliant study, States of Denial: Knowing About Atrocities and Suffering , drew on Cohen’s own reporting of cover-ups, disappearances and torture in his native South Africa. Yet its examination of the ways in which we pretend to ourselves that terrible events are not taking place was broader, taking in Latin America, the Rwanda genocide , the Holocaust, the Middle East and other examples. Cohen distinguished between the different ways in which politicians, journalists and others have suppressed knowledge of the truth. He identified what he called “literal denial” - the unblinking assertion that crimes are not taking place. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s recent speech to the United Nations contained numerous examples of literal denial. He said that the ratio of civilian casualties to combatants in Gaza was exceptionally low, that Israel did not block aid to Gaza, and that Hamas should be blamed for shortages. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); He also made the nonsensical assertion that settler violence in the occupied West Bank was down to a “handful of young juvenile delinquents”. A Palestinian proverb, Yaktheb al-kithbah wa yusadikaha, roughly translates as: “He tells a lie, and then he believes it.” It describes the mental state of someone who has repeated the same falsehood so many times that eventually he or she has come to regard it as fact. This may explain not just Netanyahu but also the army of apologists who blindly repeat what he says. Cohen also paid attention to a more sophisticated form of denial which does challenge basic facts, but instead sanitises them in ways that seem reasonable or acceptable. He called this phenomenon “interpretative denial”. Export licences Channel 4 recently published an hour-long documentary exploring how British ministers have employed the technique identified by Cohen as “interpretative denial”, to sanction Israel’s destruction of Gaza. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); It is obvious to most people that Israel regularly commits crimes against humanity, with the newest Google Maps imagery showing total devastation across the enclave. Yet throughout this period, British ministers have denied Israeli war crimes. How have they managed this level of cognitive dissonance? The Channel 4 film, Britain’s Gaza Secrets Exposed , went a long way to providing the answer. Over the past three years, British firms have exported millions of pounds worth of weaponry to Israel while it flattened Gaza and slaughtered civilians. All those weapons need export licences. Under both domestic and international law , Britain is not allowed to export weapons to any country which it has reason to suspect commits war crimes. This explains why, for the last three years, the Foreign Office unit that investigates potential breaches of humanitarian law has been busy assessing Israel’s military actions in Gaza. Channel 4 reporter Ramita Navai obtained internal Foreign Office assessments of Israel’s conduct during the early stages of the war, dealing with hundreds of notorious cases. Her investigation shows that again and again, the British Foreign Office failed to hold the Israeli army to account. It’s not just the government that is guilty of Cohen’s interpretative denial when it comes to the annihilation of Gaza. Most of the British media is equally complicit Take the case of Hind Rajab , the five-year-old girl trapped in a car with her dead family after they were shot by Israeli soldiers. She spent three hours on the telephone asking for help. Eventually, permission came for rescuers, but when they did, soldiers shot dead both the rescuers and Hind herself. Unspeakable and hideous - but the Foreign Office assessors cited insufficient evidence to conclude that Israeli soldiers had breached international law. Or take the air strike on Al-Fakhoura school in Jabalia refugee camp in November 2023, which killed dozens of people, including women and children. The Foreign Office did not label this a war crime, even though the United Nations had clearly marked the school as a shelter for displaced civilians, and its coordinates had been given to the Israeli military. British officials managed to reach the same conclusion after 48 members of the Elian family were slaughtered in Nuseirat, and after Israel targeted a Medical Aid for Palestinians compound housing four British doctors. In only one case did the Foreign Office conclude that even a “possible” breach of international law had taken place. This was the Israeli strike that killed seven World Central Kitchen charity workers, including three British citizens. Dispatches revealed that even as Israel pledged an “full, urgent and transparent” enquiry into the World Kitchen tragedy, then Foreign Secretary David Cameron was signing off yet another batch of approvals for arms exports - without waiting for the Israeli investigation to be completed. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Convenient findings There’s little question that these repeated Foreign Office judgments were convenient. Throughout this period, Britain was an enthusiastic ally of Israel, and unwilling to offend the United States . So was the British legal process twisted in Israel’s favour? Channel 4 suggests it might have been. It secured an interview with Mark Smith , the only British official to have resigned over Gaza. His comments were devastating: “We’ve all seen the aerial footage of entire neighbourhoods literally flattened to the ground. They’ve destroyed the vast majority of all residential buildings in Gaza. I’ve never seen anything like it in my career, in my life.” Smith went on: “So, even without being on the team and having access to the assessments being made, I could see, on the news, in broad daylight, with the naked eye, the most appalling attacks taking place on a daily basis. I mean, almost every single school, and almost every single hospital, in Gaza, has been damaged, or destroyed. “How are we justifying our arms exports? If there is even a question whether domestically or internationally that a state that you are selling arms to might be conducting a genocide, then the time to be discussing whether they might be in breach of IHL is way gone.” Smith says he stepped down after witnessing “illegality and complicity with war crimes” at the heart of government. Why Palestine solidarity activists must keep up pressure on UK government Read More » Channel 4 asked William Schabas, a leading human rights expert who comes from a family of Holocaust survivors, to comment on the Foreign Office’s judgement in the Hind Rajab tragedy. He replied: “When a child is killed in this manner, I think there has to be a very strong presumption that normally there cannot be any military justification or explanation for it.” Channel 4 also spoke to Dearbhla Minogue, a lawyer with the Global Legal Action Network, which alongside the Palestinian NGO Al-Haq, took the UK government to court over its weapons exports to Israel. The groups lost , but the case led to the disclosure of the Foreign Office assessments analysed by Channel 4. Minogue says that the British government used a rigged methodology which made identifying Israeli violations almost impossible. According to her, the Foreign Office legal team created a Catch 22 situation. In order to prove that a strike violated international humanitarian law, it required exact information on Israeli intentions. Since Israel refused to provide this information the Foreign Office was unable to reach a conclusion on any incident, meaning that arms sales could continue. This brings me to a final point. The Channel 4 investigation has brought into the public domain a mass of fresh information that helps us to understand British complicity in the destruction of Gaza. Yet I have not found a single mainstream media outlet reporting its revelations. The explanation for this media omerta is simple: it’s not just the British government that is guilty of Cohen’s interpretative denial when it comes to the annihilation of Gaza. Nuclear power output rises 4pc to record high. ISLAMABAD: Pakistan’s nuclear electricity production increased by 3.7 per cent to a record 22.5 terawatt-hours (TWh) in 2025, while solar power generation expanded even faster amid unaffordable overall energy prices. Pakistan’s “nuclear electricity production has increased from 21.7TWh net in 2024 to a new all-time high of 22.5TWh in 2025,” says the World Nuclear Industry Status Report (WNISR) 2026, based on data for the period ending July 2026. “For the first time, solar power generation exceeded nuclear output — and by far — with 36.3 TWh,” the report said, describing the figure as highly underestimated. The WNISR 2026 is financed by the German Federal Office for the Safety of Nuclear Waste Management, the Austrian Federal Ministry for Agriculture and Forestry, Climate and Environmental Protection, Regions and Water Management, the Greens/EFA Group in the European Parliament and the Swiss Energy Foundation. Solar generation reaches 36.3 TWh, surpassing nuclear production for first time The report noted that the US leads the world, with 94 operating reactors and a nuclear generation capacity of 96,952 megawatts (MW), followed by France with 63,000MW from 57 reactors and China with 61,521MW from 63 reactors. Despite being the pioneer in connecting nuclear power to the grid in 1954, Russia ranks fourth, with 27,969MW from 34 reactors, up from 26,800MW in 2023. Pakistan operates six nuclear reactors with a combined operating capacity of 3,262MW. All six operating reactors were built by the China National Nuclear Corporation (CNNC), including the two Hualong One reactors, Kanupp-2 (K-2) and Kanupp-3 (K-3), outside Karachi, and four 300MW Chashma nuclear reactors. The WNISR, citing the Pakistan Economic Survey 2025-26, said the country’s share of debt repayment was notable in the total cost of electricity generation from nuclear energy. The debt is mainly associated with the newly constructed K-2 and K-3 reactors, commissioned in 2022 and 2023, respectively. According to the survey, the 12-year debt repayment period “is only 20 per cent” of the reactors’ estimated economic lifetime of 60 years. The Kanupp site also houses a 90MW CANDU (K-1) reactor, which was closed in 2021 after 50 years of operation. The Chashma Nuclear Power Gener­ating Station (CNPGS) comprises four operating reactors, C-1 to C-4, with a total capacity of 1,230MW. CNNC is also building another 1,000MW Hualong One reactor at the Chashma site, known as C-5. The agreement to build the reactor dates back to 2017, but it took more than seven years to progress to formal construction. The first concrete pour for the base slab of the reactor building took place on Dec 30, 2024. C-5 is expected to be completed by 2030 and is China’s only ongoing nuclear new-build project abroad. Solar revolution The report said Pakistan’s solar revolution apparently did not reflect the full deployment of solar technology in the country. A mysterious decline in power consumption despite economic growth was later explained by import statistics: private, unregistered photovoltaic installations had enabled considerable self-consumption that did not pass through the public grid. Between the beginning of 2017 and mid-2026, Pakistan imported a cumulative total of more than 58GW of solar panels from China. Of this, 40GW, or 69pc, was imported during the two and a half years from 2024 to mid-2026. Pakistan has consequently become the second-largest single-country import market behind the Netherlands, which acts as a hub for Europe. “Pakistan installed in five years about twice as much solar capacity as France did in a decade,” the report said. In 2025, Pakistan was China’s top customer for solar panels. By summer 2025, solar had become Pakistan’s single largest source of electricity. Published in Dawn, October 5th, 2026
