Only ‘just, fair’ talks can end war, Iran tells US. TEHRAN: Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi declared on Sunday that there was no military solution to the US’ war against the Islamic Republic and that only negotiations based on “justice and fairness” could end the conflict, as talks between Washington and Tehran appeared to be at an impasse. “If our enemies again choose the path of military confrontation, our response will be stronger than before, and we will defend ourselves with even more force,” Araghchi told a gathering of foreign ambassadors in Tehran. “There is no military solution, nor any solution based on new sanctions,” he continued, adding “only negotiations based on justice and fairness” could end the conflict. Tensions continue to centre on the standoff between the US and Iran regarding the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, a critical conduit for Gulf oil and gas. Iran’s parliament speaker Mohammad Baqer Ghalibaf reiterated that the vital Strait of Hormuz will not reopen until seven Iranian conditions set out in a June interim agreement with the US are met. “The position of the Islamic Republic of Iran is completely clear and firm, and the strait of Hormuz will not be opened until our seven conditions, based on the Islamabad memorandum of understanding, are met,” he was quoted by state media as saying. Ghalibaf added that Washington “must understand that the period of dragging out the process and dictating one-sided demands is over”. Iranian and US officials held indirect talks last week on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly, during which Tehran said it presented its seven conditions. The conditions include a ceasefire across the Middle East, the unfreezing of Iranian assets abroad, the lifting of sanctions on its oil sector and an end to the US naval blockade. US President Donald Trump publicly rejected the proposal while leaving the door open to both further talks and renewed military operations. The US nonetheless replied to Tehran’s proposal last week, with Qatar shuttling messages between the two sides in an effort to end the conflict and reopen the strait. Iran’s foreign ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said that the latest US counterproposals were “more or less in line with their previous positions, specifically on the nuclear issue”, but that Tehran’s focus was on Hormuz. “We have clearly indicated that we are focusing on the issue of the Strait of Hormuz,” he said, adding that reopening the waterway required an end to disruption of Iranian maritime traffic and the lifting of sanctions. He denied that Tehran had offered UN nuclear watchdog inspections of its facilities in exchange for sanctions relief, saying Iran had not entered into nuclear discussions. The US has not struck Iran since Sept 1 but has continued a fresh military buildup. Axios reported that Washington had deployed additional Patriot missile batteries to Saudi Arabia and Qatar to protect energy facilities, and that the USS Theodore Roosevelt carrier strike group was heading to the Middle East. Iran’s army, meanwhile, said it would upgrade the range of its missiles, underlining Tehran’s warning that it is preparing for further confrontation even as it continues to call for diplomacy. Separately, Iran’s Oil Minister Mohsen Paknejad has resigned and Hamid Bovard, chief executive of the government-owned National Iranian Oil Company, will be in charge of the ministry as acting minister, state media said on Sunday, without providing a reason for the resignation. Mohsen Paknejad has been the oil mini­ster of the Opec member country since August 2024 and resigns as the seven-month war between Iran and the US puts pressure on the country’s economy. “With acceptance of Mohsen Paknejad’s resignation by Dr Pezeshkian [the country’s president], Hamid Bovard has been appointed as acting oil minister”, state media cited an official at the president’s office as saying. Paknejad was cited by state media, ahead of the news of his resignation, as saying “revenues of the oil that we have sold are still coming and that will continue God willing”. Rawalpindi traders fear road closures as PTI’s long march looms. RAWALPINDI: The failure of talks between the government and opposition PTI has raised fears of road closures in the garrison city, worrying residents, traders and students about possible disruptions in the coming days. Due to this, universities in the twin cities of Rawalpindi and Islamabad will continue their online classes amid fears of road closures in the coming week. Arid Agriculture University Rawalpindi near Faizabad will conduct online classes on Monday and is yet to decide whether on-campus classes will start or not. A senior university official told Dawn that online classes were safer as, in case of protest rallies, the administration would immediately vacate the boys’ and girls’ hostels. “It will be difficult for the university administration to ask the students to go back home for a few days,” he said, adding that after assessing the situation on Monday, a decision would be taken on starting on-campus classes. Traders urge govt, opposition to resolve their political issues and create conducive environment for business Private schools on Murree Road and 6th Road were also worried as, in case of protests, the administration would close them. “We have not completed the syllabus which was supposed to be completed before the winter vacations due to the sudden closure of schools last month,” said Mohammad Umer, the owner of a private school. When contacted, District Education Authority Chief Executive Officer Yaseen Khan Baloch said there was no notification regarding the closure of schools. “We closed schools last month but classes for 9th and 10th grades continued,” he said. He said a school on Murree Road had been handed over to the police to accommodate police personnel. “We provided the third floor of the Education Authority building to accommodate the police so that education in schools will not suffer,” he said. Traders asked the government and opposition to end their political issues and create a conducive environment for businesses, saying the threat of closure of roads and bazaars had disturbed them. Rawalpindi Anjuman Tajraan President Shahid Ghafoor Paracha said that for the last one month shopkeepers had failed to do business easily as, last week, all roads leading to Rawalpindi and Islamabad were closed, and now the PTI has started a protest march from KP which would lead to the closure of roads again. He said Rawalpindi’s trade centres catered to the twin cities, Azad Jammu and Kashmir, Gilgit-Baltistan and adjoining areas, and during such circumstances, people would not come to the bazaars and traders could not send their goods for fear that trucks would get stuck. He said inflation had already squeezed the purchasing power of people and traders had failed to do business for the last month amid the threat of protest rallies and sit-ins. According to an official, more than 43,200 police personnel have been deployed to deal with the PTI march. Of the 43,200, as many as 30,700 police personnel have been deployed in Attock, 10,600 in Rawalpindi district and 1,976 in Jhelum, Murree and Chakwal. For the accommodation of the police force, five government schools, one private school and a college in and around Taxila have been vacated. Moreover, Water and Sanitation Agency (Wasa) had sent 22 water tankers on September 22 to Taxila to cater to the police, which have not yet returned to the garrison city, disturbing the water supply system. PHC stays deportation of 86 Afghan medical students. PESHAWAR: Peshawar High Court has temporarily stopped deportation of 86 Afghan students studying in different public sector medical colleges in the province and allowed them to continue their studies. A bench consisting of Justice Wiqar Ahmad and Justice Farah Jamshed issued notices to respondents including the federal interior secretary, director general of immigration and passport and Pakistan Medical and Dental Council’s registrar, seeking their comments in a petition filed jointly by the said 86 students including Selsela Dost and others. The bench fixed Oct 12 for next hearing of the petition with the direction that in the meanwhile, petitioners should not be deported till the next date of hearing. “They shall be allowed to continue their studies, if there is no other reason for discontinuation of their studies,” the bench directed. The bench also ordered to club the instant petition with an earlier one filed by another Afghan student Seemen Noori on the same issue. Allows them to continue studies in medical colleges of KP The petitioners have sought multiple reliefs from the court, seeking declaration that the two impugned letters issued by PMDC on July 31, 2026, and Sept 1, 2026, insofar as they required the petitioners to discontinue their studies and immediately leave Pakistan, as illegal, arbitrary and of no legal effect. They sought directives of the court for medical and dental colleges in the province to allow the petitioners to smoothly continue their studies, without interruption merely on account of the impugned PMDC letters/circulars or pendency of their visa-extension applications. Advocate Waseemuddin Khattak appeared for the petitioners and stated that his clients had been granted admission against Afghan quota seats into various medical and dental colleges across Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. He stated that petitioners had been studying in different professional years in medical and dental colleges, where after Pakistan Medical and Dental Council (PMDC) by passing an impugned order had cancelled all admissions of Afghan students across the country. He pointed out that on Sept 11, 2026, Lahore High Court granted interim relief to several Afghan students studying in its jurisdiction by suspending operation on the impugned order of PMDC. Mr Khattak said that the petitioners were Afghan nationals, who lawfully entered Pakistan on valid student visas for the purpose of medical education. He stated that they were aggrieved by the unlawful interruption of their ongoing studies pursuant to the impugned letters issued by PMDC. The counsel argued that his clients had been condemned unheard and their rights to education, life and dignity had been violated as the council had transgressed its jurisdiction under PMDC Act, 2023. He said that petitioners’ fundamental rights should be treated in accordance with law. He argued that PMDC’s powers under law must be exercised within the bounds of the Constitution and Pakistan’s international legal obligations. He stated neither the 2023 Act nor constitutional or international principles permitted the council to act arbitrarily, particularly against students, who had already spent years pursuing their medical education in this province. It merits a mention that the high court has on Sept 23 stopped law enforcement agencies from arresting or deporting 17 Afghan doctors serving in two private hospitals of the provincial capital and allowed them to continue their post graduate training here. The order was issued in a petition jointly filed by 17 trainee medical officers including Mohammad Idrees and others, challenging the PMDC letters and consequential circulars issued on Sept 2, 2026, by two private hospitals for discontinuation of the petitioners’ duties/FCPS training.
