Somalia Awaits a New Security Order as Mission Drawdown Looms pfranz Fri, 09/18/2026 - 21:00 Latest Updates Africa Asia-Pacific Europe Latin America & Caribbean Middle East & North Africa United States Global Issues & Institutions My Reading List Somali police officers walk along a road median while patrolling a busy street in Mogadishu, on November 10, 2025. TONY KARUMBA / AFP Commentary / Africa 18 September 2026 16 minutes Somalia Awaits a New Security Order as Mission Drawdown Looms The multilateral missions that have helped the Somali government fight Al-Shabaab for nearly two decades may be coming to an end. Mogadishu and its partners should get started now developing a plan for what they will do next. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print Related Tags Somalia The multilateral missions that have protected Somalia’s government from the jihadist insurgent group Al-Shabaab since 2007 could be drawing to a close. In early July, the U.S. informed the African Union (AU) that it would not back an extension of the UN Support Office in Somalia (UNSOS) – which provides crucial logistical assistance to the AU’s Support and Stabilisation Mission – beyond the end of its current mandate in December. The U.S. position has subsequently softened, with U.S. diplomats telling the AU in September that Washington would consider a twelve-month extension before calling a stop to further UN aid. This development buys time for a more orderly drawdown or some kind of transition. But the reality remains inescapable: the security blanket that Somalia has lived under for almost two decades is on borrowed time. The forthcoming UN General Assembly provides a prime opportunity for the Somali government, the AU and its security partners to kickstart essential discussions about how to keep Somalia safe. Given the AU mission’s reliance on the UN to provide water, food, fuel and transport, it will almost certainly be unable to continue in anything like its present form without UN help. The AU, its foreign partners and the Somali federal government are considering how to keep the mission going, but they do not have any particularly enticing options in mind. There is no clear alternative to the UN office, whose budget is nearly half a billion dollars, when it comes to setting up, running and paying for a multinational force. That said, predictions that the prospective end of UN and possibly AU security assistance will see the government collapse and Al-Shabaab emerge victorious are wide of the mark. While Al-Shabaab remains a major threat to the Somali government and controls swathes of southern and central Somalia, the group is largely confined to rural areas. The government’s grip extends to most urban centres, with security in the capital Mogadishu improving sharply in recent years. Support from the UN has helped maintain this precarious status quo. But an end to multilateral assistance need not culminate in the federal state’s downfall, even if a mismanaged transition could spell trouble. A combination of Somali and other international forces, including those already stationed in the country, should form part of a new international security structure. It is now up to Mogadishu and its international partners to begin planning this shift before it is too late. Approximate areas of operation for AUSSOM troop contributors. Some troop contributors maintain bilateral contingents in addition to their AUSSOM deployments. Source: Crisis Group research as of September 2026. CRISIS GROUP More Trouble for a Struggling Mission The AU mission and its UN logistics support office – the mainstay of foreign assistance for Somalia’s security – rely on troops from Africa and funds from farther afield. Ugandan troops were the first to be deployed upon the mission’s launch in 2007, followed soon thereafter by forces from Burundi and Djibouti. Kenya and Ethiopia joined in 2012 and 2014, respectively, after first launching their own bilateral interventions to safeguard their borders from Al-Shabaab incursions. The mission pushed the jihadist group out of many urban centres in south-central Somalia in the 2010s, including Mogadishu in 2011. More recently, however, the AU has struggled to find money for the mission, with long-time donors like the EU whittling down their contributions and pushing for the exit door. The mission has been running a large deficit for several years, even as it has taken measures to cut spending. Troop numbers have dwindled from 22,000 in the mid-2010s to around 12,000 today. Instead of launching offensive operations deep in the hinterlands controlled by Al-Shabaab, the mission has turned more toward protecting urban areas it already holds, while playing a supporting role in Somali army campaigns. The financial crunch has since extended to the UN’s logistical support, funded through UN assessed contributions – mandatory dues paid by all member states to underwrite the global body’s operations. Even before the Trump administration took office, U.S. officials were wary of the model that sees UN finances flow to a non-UN mission, regarding it as an undesirable precedent. In early 2025, the U.S. blocked a proposal for the AU mission to also receive funding through UN assessed contributions, arguing in part that the UN is already spending heavily on UNSOS. In September 2025, the U.S. shelved planned contributions to the UN peacekeeping budget, including for UNSOS. Hence, its refusal to support the office’s existence any further does not come as a complete surprise. Much as Washington has no wish to see an Al-Shabaab resurgence, it seems to be pulling the plug on a setup that has done much to keep the group in check. Much as Washington has no wish to see an Al-Shabaab resurgence, it seems to be pulling the plug on a setup that has done much to keep the group in check. Despite this apparent contradiction, the U.S. government believes that the status quo is no longer tenable: the multilateral missions are not as effective as they once were, while the Somali government should bear the primary responsibility for leading the fight with Al-Shabaab. U.S. diplomats believe that Somali elites are skirting their duties, preoccupied with pursuing political vendettas rather than combating jihadists. It is difficult to know if President Donald Trump’s evident personal animus toward Somalia has also played a role. A number of U.S. officials agree that ending UNSOS, and by extension threatening the existence of the AU mission, is a risk. It was probably for this reason that the U.S. backtracked in September to grant the UN mission an additional twelve months to draw down. But this move only defers rather than eliminates the challenges ahead. The U.S. argues that Mogadishu can keep Al-Shabaab at bay by enhancing the deployment of Somali forces, and combining this measure with assistance from abroad, including troops from neighbouring countries and air support from the U.S. and Türkiye. The U.S. says it remains ready to contribute to fighting Al-Shabaab. It just no longer wants to do so through a multilateral vehicle that it regards as an unnecessary expense. Are There Alternatives to UNSOS? The drawdown and eventual closure of UNSOS would, in effect, mean that the AU mission could not continue as currently designed. The UN mission keeps AU troops supplied with food, water and fuel, sustaining nearly 50 bases across southern Somalia. It also provides transport for AU deployments. When funds permit, it supports Somali soldiers operating alongside the AU personnel. Privately, AU officials say the mission cannot continue without UN support: one termed the U.S. decision on the UNOSOS mandate “life-threatening”. Even with a twelve-month stay of execution, the UN support office’s coming year will be focused on winding down its extensive logistical responsibilities. Deciding what comes next has become imperative for the Somali authorities. A few options for logistical assistance for the AU mission have been mooted, but all face serious drawbacks. In July, the Somali government, the AU and troop-contributing states met in the Ugandan capital Kampala to discuss the mission’s future. They endorsed a plan for uninterrupted support for another eighteen to 24 months, a period that would be used to carry out offensives against Al-Shabaab and a more gradual drawdown. For Washington, however, an extension of UN support beyond what is now on the table is out of the question, a stance it communicated in September. Another option would be for the AU to use the time UNSOS has left to replace it with an AU logistical mission. Another option would be for the AU to use the time UNSOS has left to replace it with an AU logistical mission. But given the AU’s lack of experience in running such a complex operation, this option appears unworkable in the near term. The AU could subcontract logistics to a private company, but diplomats note that it would take up to two years to establish a mission with capabilities similar to those of UNSOS. Even if it were possible, the financial crunch would not vanish. With the AU mission unable even to cover troop stipends, there is no way at present that it could shoulder the costs of logistics. The deeper pockets of partners alarmed by the possibility of an imminent worsening of Somali security, such as the EU or Gulf Arab countries, might be prised open to an extent. But with so many other crises competing for resources, a donor boost remains a long shot. Alternatively, the AU could take whatever funding is available from the EU and others, channelling it toward covering troop stipends and the logistics of a smaller mission. This option would enable the AU to maintain its presence, but only by sacrificing its operational clout, perhaps by retrenching at a few key locations, most likely in and around Mogadishu and regional capitals. But countries contributing troops to the AU mission already argue they do not have enough personnel to protect themselves, let alone undertake forward operations. Reducing their numbers further could end up at a point where the mission is unable to defend itself or others from Al-Shabaab attack. With limited funding committed for 2026 and nothing beyond that, the AU might also find it difficult to win donors over to the idea of supporting a less effective version of the same mission. A further variant of this option is being floated in Addis Ababa, where the AU has its headquarters: reconfiguring the mission under a new regional mechanism, but still with an AU mandate. In this scenario, many of the African troops deployed in Somalia would stay, but under a setup not unlike the Multinational Joint Task Force in the Lake Chad basin, a regional initiative to combat Boko Haram. Parallels with the Lake Chad basin are imperfect, however: the various national militaries operating there largely do so inside their own frontiers, coordinating more on cross-border matters. The proposal also offers little by way of a solution to the logistics and funding dilemmas, simply passing the buck to troop-contributing states. One or another of these options might emerge to enable Somalia’s multilateral security support to stagger on past 2027. The U.S. decision to grant an extra twelve months buys time to evaluate all the options and allows for less haste in the overhaul. But one way or another, a transition, with all its uncertainties, appears imminent. Turning to Somali Forces The AU’s exit strategy is premised on Somali forces standing ready to take the mission’s place when it finally shuts down. There is no doubt that the Somali National Army has boosted its strength in recent years, generating upward of 10,000 new troops under training schemes supported by foreign partners like Türkiye, the United Arab Emirates and Eritrea. But it is still ill-prepared to fully and rapidly take the AU mission’s place. Certain areas handed over by the mission to Somali forces in recent years have later fallen into Al-Shabaab’s hands. Even when the Somali army has led operations against Al-Shabaab, such as in Lower Shabelle in 2025-2026, it has remained dependent on external support. Somali officials have argued for many years that they can take full responsibility for security, but that they need more time. Many in the current government and its predecessors have wanted Somali forces to step up, only to find themselves hamstrung by political rifts within the federal system that have weakened the national security apparatus. State-level forces are generally underdeveloped, while the divisions between federal officials and leaders in Puntland and Jubaland, who are at loggerheads over how power and resources are divided in Somalia’s federal system, hinder the emergence of a unified national army. During times of political crisis, such as the election-related turmoil at present, federal and state forces sometimes turn their guns on each other. These shortcomings have driven Mogadishu to establish a series of bilateral security agreements with Uganda, Kenya and Ethiopia, ensuring that their troops will stay despite the AU mission’s withdrawal. Uganda reportedly has a force of around 2,000 troops stationed in and around Mogadishu, while Kenya and Ethiopia retain larger contingents closer to their own borders. Bilateral foreign forces in Somalia have remained stable even as the AU mission shrinks, a trend that will probably continue after its eventual departure. What Could a New Security Approach Look Like? The AU mission’s future is for now unclear. While replacing support from the UN, and possibly finding a substitute for the mission, would undoubtedly be a huge undertaking, the situation is not hopeless. With proper planning, political leadership and a measure of continued foreign backing, the Somali government should be able to shift from dependence on a multilateral force to a series of bilateral relationships that prevent a major security breakdown and sweeping military gains by Al-Shabaab. That said, there is little doubt that the impending loss of the UN support office’s annual spending on Somali security needs will cause headaches. Even if the AU manages somehow to retain a presence, the most likely shape of Somalia’s future security support will derive chiefly from the deeply rooted interests of Mogadishu’s foreign partners. Key members of the AU mission, particularly Kenya and Ethiopia, are primarily motivated by border security, particularly the desire to maintain a buffer against Al-Shabaab. Uganda’s President Yoweri Museveni views his country’s longstanding deployment as a key part of his legacy. He likely holds out hope that Mogadishu will be able to find a donor to pay for Ugandan units stationed around the capital. From outside the region, Türkiye has become Somalia’s most important bilateral partner in recent years, training thousands of Somali troops as well as deploying advanced military assets like drones and F-16s. Ankara also remains keen to protect its wide-ranging strategic investments in the country. The U.S., for its part, asserts that it will, for now, maintain its bilateral counter-terrorism operations, particularly its drone program. Making full use of these various bilateral arrangements is the most pragmatic way to go about preventing a serious deterioration in security after UNSOS closes. Making full use of these various bilateral arrangements is the most pragmatic way to go about preventing a serious deterioration in security after UNSOS closes, regardless of what happens to the AU mission, while buying more time for the Somali military to assume greater responsibility. The AU mission’s major troop contributors would ideally keep most of their contingents where they are, arranging their own logistics in the process, but changes are likely. The loss of UNSOS assistance will probably spur Kenya and Ethiopia into consolidating positions nearer their own borders, while Uganda will probably focus more on protecting Mogadishu and its environs. Smaller troop contributors like Burundi and Djibouti, on the other hand, may be less inclined to continue without additional support. In areas where foreign troops do withdraw, Somali forces should prepare to take over. Mogadishu claimed in early August that it has 14,000 troops available for military operations, who could instead be deployed as holding forces to take the place of departing AU personnel. Somali troops tend not to be as well trained or equipped as their AU counterparts, however, making a one-to-one switch from AU to Somali soldiers a hazardous proposition. Taking these steps might contain Al-Shabaab to its rural bastions and avoid the loss of major cities. Proper coordination with bilateral forces could help protect the most strategically important areas, including towns, infrastructure and supply routes. But a modest fallback from some of the positions that are now under the AU mission’s control seems inevitable. Uganda, for example, maintains more than a dozen bases in the Lower Shabelle region, which will be difficult to hold without UNSOS logistical support. Smaller towns surrounded by Al-Shabaab, such as Qoryoley, could be at risk of falling to the insurgents once the AU pulls out. Parts of Hirshabelle would also be vulnerable due to the concentration of Al-Shabaab forces in the area since 2025, adding pressure to towns along the main road in the state, such as Jalalaqsi. Even small losses could give momentum back to Al-Shabaab, while the capture of roads and economic centres would help sustain the group financially. It may be possible over the coming years to keep parts of the battlefield tilted in the Somali authorities’ favour through the calibrated deployment of foreign troops, especially when it comes to the defence of urban centres and transport arteries. Still, the systemic challenges to Somali security thrown up by a radical change in security arrangements cannot be wished away. If they are left unaddressed, the danger will rise of greater government losses and an Al-Shabaab surge outside its rural strongholds. First, shifting the security burden onto African states will not resolve the funding problem unless donors and Somali officials take bold steps. If the AU wants to remain involved, it will have to do more to raise its own funds. If not, the AU mission’s current backers – primarily the EU and UK, which in 2025 together contributed approximately $90 million – could find ways to transfer this support to cover logistics and stipends for troop-contributing states from the region and Somali forces. Gulf Arab states, which number among Somalia’s key backers, may even be more inclined to support bilateral forces, viewing multilateral support as a poor investment because it translates into minimal diplomatic influence. Even though its resources are strained, the Somali government could also reduce the burden on foreign donors: the government has managed to raise domestic revenue in recent years and has even funded a number of internal military operations and deployments. The more it can take on, the less it will need to lobby the same donors on behalf of other African troop contributors. Secondly, the Somali government, troop-contributing countries and donors will need a forum in which to debate the country’s security needs and priorities. Security coordination within the AU mission has often proven a challenge, but the mission’s guiding framework helped ensure that its contributors adhered to a basic common strategy. The government should now establish a new forum that would meet regularly to coordinate with its bilateral partners, enabling Mogadishu to impress upon them the country’s main security requirements and hopefully curbing the pursuit of individual interests by troop-contributing states. Somalia’s security partners in turn should focus on fulfilling their security roles and avoid meddling in local politics in their areas of operation. A forum could also be an opportunity for the government to detail a national plan for Somalia’s future security, which would help assuage local concerns that a transition might leave some parts of the country better protected than others. Without effective coordination, bilateral security relationships could hasten the country’s fragmentation by fracturing it into various zones of influence that overlap with Somalia’s current divisions between the federal authorities and assertive member states. Furthermore, there is a risk that powerful partners might look to Mogadishu to provide exclusive concessions – economic or otherwise – in return for military assistance. Better coordination with multiple partners will help the Somali authorities handle these demands and keep the focus on making the country safe. With negotiations on the AU mission’s next mandate set to kick off at the UN Security Council by December, Somalia would benefit greatly from having a plan and buy-in from security partners in place by then. What Should Happen Now? Somalia’s multilateral security system has been limping toward its finale for several years. Establishing a new model without the UN support office and possibly the AU mission will be arduous; a series of bilateral security relationships is unlikely to match what multilateral deployments have achieved. Current funding and geopolitical realities, however, make this shift the most realistic option beyond 2027. The government should be using the time it has to make this change work. A clear grasp of the challenges ahead would be a good place to start. Diplomats from some of Mogadishu’s security partners say both the government and the AU expect that further compromises can be hammered out over the future of UNSOS. If so, that confidence is misplaced. The Trump administration appears intent on seeing the end of the UN support mission, even if it has signalled that more time is available to allow for a smoother transition. It is also hard to gauge how much UNSOS will be able to do in 2027 as it focuses on its liquidation. Rather than assume business as usual, Mogadishu and its partners should use the temporary reprieve they have been granted to construct a new security system that can kick into action as early as the second half of 2027. The Somali government should urgently convene its security partners to establish a broad division of responsibilities and priorities to follow the departure of UNSOS. Setting out a viable plan for the country after UN support winds down also has a better chance of attracting fresh donor backing. A shift primarily to bilateral support is still a temporary measure, and it should only buy time for a lasting solution to the country’s troubles: a Somali government that can manage its own security needs. Mogadishu’s shortcoming in achieving this goal, despite two decades of foreign support, is rooted in entrenched political divisions rather than just financial and technical challenges. In the short term, the government should be ready to deploy troops to areas likely to be vacated by foreign troops; it should launch major new offensives only once the transition has been consolidated. But for the security transition to work over the long term, Somalia’s government and political class must address their political divisions and row in the same direction. They could start to do so by resolving the dispute regarding the timing and format for elections, continuing by concluding these polls swiftly so that an incoming administration with a clear mandate can take office. The new administration should make preparing for a security transition an overriding priority. It should lay out a plan for how Somali forces can take over from foreign troops, including by bringing federal member states into discussions regarding the future of Somali security. Such a plan is the best way to realise the country’s full sovereignty – an oft-stated ambition of the Somali government. But the longer political disputes drag on, the greater the risk that the transition to Somali forces falters and Al-Shabaab resurges. The U.S. decision to pull the plug on UNSOS appears to be a defining act in the decline of Somalia’s multilateral security system. In its aftermath, short-term gains by Al-Shabaab look inevitable. But a well-managed transition should help mitigate any losses and lay the groundwork for Somalia’s eventual stability. Shrink the UN mloukili Mon, 09/21/2026 - 15:05 Latest Updates Africa Asia-Pacific Europe Latin America & Caribbean Middle East & North Africa United States Global Issues & Institutions My Reading List Op-Ed / Global 21 September 2026 1 minutes Shrink the UN Originally published in Foreign Affairs The Next Secretary-General Must Get Back to Basics Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print Richard Gowan Program Director, Global Issues and Institutions https://twitter.com/RichardGowan1 Related Tags Multilateral Diplomacy The United Nations, international officials sometimes joke, is always in crisis. Since its inception in 1945, the organization has had to navigate deep geopolitical tensions, devastating humanitarian disasters, and periodic budget shortfalls. But as world leaders gather in New York for the annual General Assembly high-level week, the UN appears to be in particularly bad shape. China, Russia, and the United States, three of the five veto-wielding powers that dominate the Security Council, have prevented it from acting on wars in Iran and Ukraine and civil conflicts in Myanmar and Sudan. Poor countries complain that donor states have not met their UN pledges on development spending. And the Trump administration halted most U.S. funding to UN activities last year, forcing the organization to cut back on its peacekeeping and relief efforts. With challenges mounting, an upcoming leadership transition may decide whether the UN can stabilize itself and perhaps even regain some credibility—or slide further into decrepitude. Current Secretary-General António Guterres plans to step down at the end of the year, having struggled to reverse the organization’s political fortunes in his decadelong tenure. He has spent much of his last two years in office grappling with staff reductions and other cost-cutting measures to ensure the UN secretariat does not go bankrupt on his watch. His has been a thankless task, but diplomats and UN officials hope a new leader will be able to take a longer-term approach to refreshing the institution and keeping governments committed to multilateralism. The small crop of candidates to succeed Guterres include senior UN trade official Rebeca Grynspan, Director General of the International Atomic Energy Agency Rafael Grossi, and Guyana’s Ambassador to the UN Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett. Regardless of who wins, Guterres' successor will need to develop a new playbook for revitalizing the organization. Any serious effort must acknowledge an unpleasant reality: as long as the world remains competitive and chaotic, the UN’s ability to forge wide-ranging international agreements will remain constrained. The Houthis’ Advance to Bab al-Mandab: Has Yemen’s War Returned? eschelhaas Tue, 09/22/2026 - 20:06 Latest Updates Africa Asia-Pacific Europe Latin America & Caribbean Middle East & North Africa United States Global Issues & Institutions My Reading List Event Recording / Middle East & North Africa 22 September 2026 1 minutes The Houthis’ Advance to Bab al-Mandab: Has Yemen’s War Returned? In this online event, Crisis Group and external experts discussed how the front collapsed so quickly and whether Saudi Arabia, the Yemeni government and Yemen’s neighbours can keep this round of fighting from sliding into a wider war. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print Related Tags Yemen Saudi Arabia Over the past week, the Houthis have swept down Yemen’s western coast and reached Bab al-Mandab, unravelling a defensive line that had held for years, and exposing just how fragmented the government camp’s forces had become. A string of retreats was decisive, as the National Resistance, Giants Brigades and other nominally allied units, each with its own command and backers, lost Khokha, Mokha and the roads linking Taiz, Hodeida and the coast, fighting side by side but never as one army. A foothold near one of the world’s busiest shipping chokepoints gives the Houthis fresh leverage over Saudi Arabia, just as Riyadh’s containment strategy is under strain. On Our Radar eschelhaas Fri, 09/25/2026 - 00:00 Latest Updates Africa Asia-Pacific Europe Latin America & Caribbean Middle East & North Africa United States Global Issues & Institutions My Reading List Special Coverage / Global 25 September 2026 20+ minutes On Our Radar On Our Radar scans conflicts and crises around the globe every week and features some of the hotspots Crisis Group’s analysts are closely watching. Whether an under-reported trend or a headline-grabbing development, our field experts explain why it matters or what should be done. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print 25 September 2026 SOUTH SUDAN President Salva Kiir dissolved South Sudan’s transitional unity government Tuesday, three months before elections scheduled for 22 December, dismantling key power-sharing institutions established under the 2018 peace agreement. Following a hurriedly passed amendment to the National Elections Act, Kiir dismissed all five vice presidents, including his long-time rival First Vice President Riek Machar, and installed a caretaker government composed entirely of loyalists. Crisis Group expert Daniel Akech says the changes allow Kiir to concentrate authority in his hands. Greater control of state institutions could help him retain power, through either a stage-managed election or a delay that prolongs his administration. The resulting political exclusion risks provoking greater conflict in an already deeply fractured country. UNITED NATIONS World leaders met this week in New York for the UN General Assembly’s annual high-level session. Crisis Group expert Daniel Forti says the week’s events proved that states still value the UN as a forum for discussing global concerns, even if common ground between them remains elusive. Some countries expect the next Secretary-General to single-handedly get the UN back on track and provide solutions for crises around the world. That attitude is short-sighted. The UN needs the conviction of its members to tackle global risks from deadly conflict to artificial intelligence. Whether states choose to work together – or continue down the path of international fragmentation – will determine whether the next decade at the UN is defined by diplomacy or disorder. U.S. - CHINA President Donald Trump hosted Chinese leader Xi Jinping for a state visit in Washington this week. Xi touted their personal rapport, called for “healthy” bilateral competition “within bounds” and argued that U.S.-China cooperation is needed to address most global challenges. Crisis Group expert Ali Wyne says the summit’s outcome was modest: the two leaders agreed to extend by two months the trade truce that they blessed in Busan, South Korea last October; it was due to expire on 10 November. They do not appear to have made a breakthrough on managing cross-strait ties, spurring diplomacy to end the U.S.-Iran war or erecting guardrails around artificial intelligence. China’s readout called on the U.S. to “adhere to the correct position of opposing ‘Taiwan independence’”, incorrectly but provocatively implying that the U.S. had changed its longstanding position (that it “does not support” that outcome). 18 September 2026 DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO Protesters streamed into the streets of Kinshasa Tuesday to decry the government’s proposals to change the constitution by popular referendum. One person was killed in clashes with police who intervened to stop the marchers from reaching parliament. Crisis Group expert Richard Moncrieff says the government’s main aim in trying to alter the constitution is to revise the clause imposing a two-term limit on presidents, thereby allowing the incumbent Félix Tshisekedi to stand for a third term. Tshisekedi is keen to hold the referendum soon, despite the opposition, because he senses that the country’s political balance has tilted in his favour. Going ahead with this vote may prove unwise, however, even if it comes off fairly smoothly. It may produce an illusion of political stability that, in turn, deflects attention from urgent tasks like reducing poverty among ordinary Congolese and taming the interlinked wars raging in the eastern provinces. MALI Algerian Prime Minister Sifi Ghrieb visited Bamako Monday in the latest sign of rapprochement between Algeria and Mali, whose relations had deteriorated badly in recent years. Crisis Group expert Jean-Hervé Jezequel says the thaw is welcome news for the Malian authorities. Bamako has been struggling to contain an insurgency linked to al-Qaeda, Jamaat Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin (JNIM), which killed 50 Malian soldiers in its latest attack on an army base last week. JNIM has lately allied with northern separatists who have also been fighting the Malian army. Historically, Algiers has been an important mediator between Bamako and northern armed groups. The warming of Algeria-Mali relations raises hopes that it might again play such a role, though maybe a more limited one given the Malian authorities’ increasingly sovereignist mindset. It could nevertheless help mitigate the conflict that has torn at Mali since 2012. PHILIPPINES Regional parliamentary elections took place on Monday in the Bangsamoro, the swathe of the southern Philippines that won autonomy in 2019 as part of a 2014 peace agreement between Manila and the Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF). At least five people were killed and twenty injured during the vote, though violence was less widespread than feared, with incidents concentrated in a few locations. No party secured an absolute majority, meaning that politicians will likely need to form a coalition. Crisis Group expert Georgi Engelbrecht says the incoming government, slated for inauguration by 30 October, will likely pair former MILF rebels with representatives of the region’s traditional political clans, unless the ex-insurgents, who have split into two factions, can reunite. The elections were a big step forward for the Bangsamoro peace process, with all eyes now on a crucial meeting between national government and MILF delegations to discuss gaps in fulfilling the 2014 accord’s terms. 11 September 2026 IRAN The International Atomic Energy Agency referred Iran to the UN Security Council Wednesday for breaching its nuclear non-proliferation obligations, marking the first time in twenty years the organisation has taken such a step. Tehran condemned the decision, blaming U.S. and Israeli strikes on its nuclear facilities for disrupting the agency’s inspections. Crisis Group expert Naysan Rafati says concerns about Iran’s lacklustre cooperation with the UN watchdog have been mounting for years, capped by over a year of blocked access to key sites bombed by the U.S. and Israel in June 2025. Given that UN sanctions were already reinstated last year, and the expectation that China and Russia will shield it from additional punitive measures at the Security Council, the referral may harden Iran’s obduracy rather than cajole it into overdue cooperation. LEBANON Israel stepped up its attacks in southern Lebanon over the weekend with strikes that killed nearly 30 people and wounded dozens more. While Israel claimed that it had targeted Hizbollah arms caches and military installations, the assaults killed several children and medical staff. Crisis Group expert David Wood says Israel’s lethal escalation could continue, unless it faces strong pressure from the U.S., its most important ally, to desist. Washington sponsored a Lebanon-Israel ceasefire struck in late June but, over two months later, the deal remains largely unfulfilled, with Israeli military action continuing and Hizbollah refusing to disarm. SOMALIA Somali piracy has seen an uptick this year, with at least six hijackings of cargo ships and smaller vessels since April. The turmoil resulting from the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran has created opportune conditions for pirates, with fewer naval patrols off the Somali coast and more commercial traffic in nearby waters as ships are diverted from the Bab al-Mandab and the Strait of Hormuz. Crisis Group expert Omar Mahmood says the number of pirate attacks is far below what it was during the heyday of Red Sea piracy fifteen years ago. The current trajectory is concerning, however, and more raids are bound to occur, absent international and local measures both offshore and on land to combat the phenomenon. 4 September 2026 HAITI Armed gang members stormed the commune of Kenscoff, overlooking Port-au-Prince, overnight on 23-24 August, killing at least 47 people and abducting more than 50, whom they threatened to kill if security forces go after the gang in that area. At least thirteen abductees have subsequently been released. Briefing the UN Security Council on 28 August, UN envoy Carlos Ruiz Massieu said the UN-backed Gang Suppression Force (GSF) would beef up its presence in the capital, while Haitian units would send reinforcements to Kenscoff. He also urged the GSF, which remains far short of its planned 5,500-person strength, to deploy in full without delay. Crisis Group expert Diego Da Rin says the Kenscoff massacre is the latest indication that gangs are on the offensive as the GSF assembles. U.S. - IRAN After a month-long lull, the U.S. resumed attacks on Iranian soil over the weekend, first striking rocket launchers on Larak island that Washington said were preparing to deploy sea mines, then hitting dozens of military targets along Iran’s southern coast. Tehran responded with missile and drone fire at bases hosting U.S. forces in the Gulf. Crisis Group expert Naysan Rafati says the uptick comes as the Trump administration tries to isolate Tehran financially through increased sanctions and a naval blockade, while in parallel undermining Iranian efforts to control the Strait of Hormuz by escorting vessels through the waterway. While Washington's approach is to squeeze wherever possible and strike whenever it deems necessary – for example, in response to Iranian strikes or efforts to rebuild its military capabilities – the Islamic Republic could counter with additional strikes of its own on U.S. assets and allies, along with further attacks on shipping. THAILAND Overnight on 22 August, militants in Thailand’s three southernmost provinces staged over 50 attacks in four hours, including bombings and arson attempts at local administrative offices, shops and other buildings. Three passersby were injured. Further incidents followed on 23 and 29 August despite tightened security. Authorities blamed Barisan Revolusi Nasional Patani Melayu (Patani-Malay National Revolutionary Front, BRN), which has fought Bangkok’s rule since 2004. Such coordinated attacks are routine, says Crisis Group expert Matt Wheeler, but the scale of this campaign was unusual. It was likely intended to discredit the state, demonstrate insurgents’ reach and heighten pressure on the government to resume peace talks that have occurred intermittently since 2013. Thailand’s chief negotiator has reportedly proposed bringing technical-level talks with BRN forward from October to this month, in part to determine the reasons for the attacks. 21 August 2026 CHINA - SOUTH KOREA Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi paid a two-day visit to South Korea this week to discuss bilateral ties, Korean peninsula tensions and broader Asian affairs. The trip came three days after U.S. President Donald Trump ordered the Pentagon to scale back joint military exercises with South Korea. Trump also said he is willing to meet with North Korean leader Kim Jong-un, as he did during his first term. These two unilateral announcements in turn prompted South Korean President Lee Jae-myung to reiterate his call for Seoul to bolster its own defences, for instance by acquiring nuclear-powered submarines and regaining independent control of its military in the event of hostilities. (Its forces would now be under U.S. command in a wartime contingency.) Crisis Group expert William Yang says the U.S.-South Korean friction has given Beijing an opening to deepen its own engagement with Seoul. It may now seek to present itself as the main mediator on the Korean peninsula, given its links with Pyongyang. ISRAEL - SYRIA Israeli warplanes bombed the Abu al-Duhur air base in northern Syria early Tuesday morning, in what Israel said was a warning against “deployment” of Turkish military personnel at the site. No casualties were reported. In remarks protesting the strike, Syrian Foreign Minister Assad al-Shaibani said Turkish officers had visited the base three days previously, but only for “training” purposes as Syrian forces refurbish the base. Tom Barrack, the U.S. ambassador to Türkiye who doubles as envoy for Syria, described Israel’s action as “unnecessary”. The backdrop, says Crisis Group expert Noah Bonsey, is an impasse in Israeli-Syrian talks about a bilateral security agreement. In these U.S.-mediated negotiations, under way since last summer, the Syrian government is seeking Israel’s withdrawal from parts of southern Syria it has occupied since December 2024, while Israel presses for limits on Turkish support for the Syrian military, among other security guarantees. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has pledged to retain a “buffer zone” in Syria as he campaigns for re-election in October. SOMALIA Local paramilitaries clashed with federal forces Monday in Baidoa, capital of Southwest state, leaving 30 dead, according to the Somali government. The militia is loyal to Abdiaziz Hassan Mohamed “Lafta-Gareen”, a former state president whom Mogadishu forcibly removed in March after a disagreement over state elections. Lafta-Gareen fled to the Kenyan capital Nairobi, but his followers have been seeking to reinstate him, making regular incursions into Baidoa from a base on its northern outskirts. They reject the new state president who took office after a hastily organised vote following Lafta-Gareen’s ouster. Crisis Group expert Omar Mahmood says Monday’s attack was the largest and deadliest to date. Calm has since returned to Baidoa, but absent an initiative to address lingering grievances over the political transition in Southwest state, further violence is likely. 14 August 2026 IRAN - U.S. Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis attacked a merchant vessel Tuesday near the Bab al-Mandab Strait, killing six people aboard, as the U.S. fired two missiles at a cargo ship in the Gulf of Oman to enforce its renewed blockade of Iran-bound maritime traffic. The strikes came as both U.S. President Donald Trump and Iran claimed to have “total control” over the Strait of Hormuz. The Islamic Republic and Oman are in negotiations over a deal to partially reopen this crucial waterway. Crisis Group expert Naysan Rafati says these consultations are part of a scramble by mediators to nudge the U.S. and Iran back into a truce, without which any bilateral understanding about the strait is unlikely to get much traction. SUDAN The paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and allied militias made rapid gains in Blue Nile state this week, taking Geissan town from the Sudanese army Tuesday and advancing into Kurmuk town Wednesday. The RSF appeared to use Ethiopian territory to launch the attacks on the two towns, both of which sit along the border with Ethiopia. Crisis Group expert Alan Boswell says the latest clashes will further drive up tensions between Sudan’s army and Addis Ababa, which accuse each other of supporting their domestic foes. Just two weeks earlier, clashes broke out between the Ethiopian military and opposing Tigray forces along a different part of the Sudan-Ethiopia border. WEST BANK Israeli settlers accompanied by soldiers besieged Palestinians in homes near the village of Qusra Sunday, among them Palestinians with U.S. citizenship. Only after four days and under U.S. pressure did the Israeli army intervene – not to chase away the settlers, but to remove a number of the Palestinians. It is another incident revealing the current Israeli government’s agenda for the West Bank, says Crisis Group expert Mairav Zonszein. The government is grabbing land, not only to create facts on the ground that will be hard for any successor to reverse, but to drive Palestinians into isolated, shrinking enclaves. 7 August 2026 CEUTA More than a hundred people died last week when Moroccan authorities apparently loosened controls along the border with Ceuta, a Spanish-administered enclave at the north-eastern tip of Morocco on the Strait of Gibraltar, unleashing an unprecedented rush of would-be emigrants into the territory. Most of those who perished were trying to swim or wade around coastal breakwaters. Following a swift Spanish military deployment, the vast majority of those who entered were returned or voluntarily went back to Morocco within days. Migrant testimony and video footage suggests that Moroccan security services helped facilitate the influx, says Crisis Group expert Riccardo Fabiani. They have previously used the spectre of unregulated migration to strong-arm Madrid into supporting Rabat’s claim to Western Sahara. Why they would use it this time is unclear. A few possible explanations come to mind: to impress upon Spain that its claim to Ceuta (which Morocco disputes) is hard to defend; to remind Madrid that it needs Rabat to protect its interests; and to earn credit with two allies, Israel and the U.S., with which the Spanish government has been at odds over Gaza and the war with Iran. CHAD The Chadian government filed a letter with the UN in late July declaring its intent to withdraw from the International Criminal Court (ICC). It is the fourth African country to take this step since 2025, after Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger. All have cited perceived anti-African bias, pointing to the fact that most of the ICC’s recent probes have focused on African countries. The Trump administration, which has sanctioned the ICC for its investigation of Israeli actions in Gaza, called on more African nations to “reclaim their sovereignty” by following in Chad’s footsteps. Crisis Group expert Enrica Picco says some Chadians will welcome N’djamena’s move on these grounds. Many, however, will see it as a way to curry favour with Washington to secure its help in counter-terrorism efforts around Lake Chad. Still others – especially among the Zaghawa ethnic group – may espy a government attempt to escape international scrutiny for complicity in crimes in neighbouring Sudan. N’djamena is accused of allowing the United Arab Emirates to funnel arms to the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces, who have massacred Zaghawa and others in Darfur. ETHIOPIA Hundreds of people have fled into Sudan after clashes last weekend in Shererina, a western district of Ethiopia’s northernmost Tigray province. The fighting flared up along the Ethiopia-Sudan border between the Ethiopian army and forces loyal to the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF). It quickly subsided, but not before raising fears of renewed open hostilities between these two sides, which fought a bloody war from 2020 to 2022. Tensions between the TPLF and Addis Ababa have been rising for months, especially after it ousted an interim regional administration established under a 2022 peace deal and reinstalled its own chair as regional president in April. The two sides now accuse each other of soliciting help from one of the main belligerents in Sudan. Independent details of the clashes are scarce, says Crisis Group expert Alan Boswell, but clearly neither side wanted to escalate further at this time. Nevertheless, the border confrontation shows how dangerous the standoff has become. 24 July 2026 THAILAND Militants attacked a checkpoint in Narathiwat, a province on the Malaysian border, on Wednesday, killing four paramilitaries, known as rangers, and an army senior non-commissioned officer. Six assailants in the bed of a pickup truck fired assault rifles and threw pipe bombs, stealing the rangers’ weapons and body armour before fleeing. They also wounded six civilians, including three children, one seriously. The army’s chief of staff, General Chaiyapruek Duangpraphat, used unusually strong language afterward, saying, “I will have my men hunt [the perpetrators] down in every village and forested mountain area. Let those who provide shelter and the countries that harbour them know this”. Crisis Group expert Matt Wheeler says attacks are routine in the country’s deep south, which has been troubled by an insurgency since 2004. These incidents rarely grab national attention, but this one is distinctive for the high death toll and the popular anger excited by widely viewed video footage of what happened. U.S. - IRAN The U.S. and Iran continued to trade blows this week, putting Washington’s Middle Eastern allies in the crosshairs of Iranian drone and missile launch teams while U.S. forces enforced a renewed naval blockade of Iran and conducted daily strikes on sites inside the country. On Wednesday, President Donald Trump pledged to “destroy one bridge or power plant” every time Tehran fires at a vessel transiting the Strait of Hormuz – a threat quickly met by warnings of retaliation in kind by the Islamic Republic. Crisis Group expert Ali Vaez says both sides appear convinced that inflicting greater physical damage and economic pain plays to their strengths, even at the risk of significant escalation. For now, this dynamic is persisting despite efforts by mediators to dial down tensions. YEMEN The Houthi rebels declared a “maritime embargo” on Saudi Arabia Monday, vowing to strike any Saudi-linked vessel passing from the Red Sea through Bab al-Mandab, the strait connecting those waters to the Gulf of Oman. A de facto truce had held between the Houthis and the Saudi-led coalition backing Yemen’s internationally recognised government from 2022 until last week, when Saudi warplanes bombed the Sanaa airport and the Houthis fired missiles at the kingdom in respo nse. On Wednesday, Saudi officials said an oil tanker caught fire after the Houthis struck it near the kingdom’s Red Sea port of Jizan. The foreign ministry in Riyadh said Saudi Arabia would take all necessary measures to defend itself, while U.S. President Donald Trump said the U.S. would inflict “major military punishment” upon both the Houthis and their ally Iran if they attack shipping again. Crisis Group expert Ahmed Nagi says the risk of open hostilities, both in the Red Sea and along front lines in Yemen, is rising dramatically. 17 July 2026 CUBA Cuba’s power grid collapsed Tuesday for the third time in less than ten days and the sixth time so far in 2026. The island’s severe energy shortages began in January when the U.S. imposed an oil blockade, triggering a humanitarian crisis. The blockade is part of the Trump administration’s pressure campaign to bring about wholesale political and economic change in Cuba, as negotiations between the two countries stall. Crisis Group expert Renata Segura says the U.S. appears to be using civilian pain as a weapon in its effort to oust Cuba’s communist regime. Havana should pursue meaningful and much needed reforms, regardless of what the U.S. does. But in the meantime Washington should lift the blockade so as not to create a humanitarian crisis in the pursuit of its goals, and avoid any further escalation. IRAN One month on, the 17 June memorandum of understanding that was to halt hostilities between the U.S. and Iran looks moribund. U.S. forces have been conducting near-daily strikes in Iran throughout the past week and resumed their blockade of Iranian shipping, while Iran has been firing drones and missiles at U.S. bases around the Gulf and in Jordan. Crisis Group expert Naysan Rafati says that both sides remain nominally open to diplomacy. But the latest exchanges underscore a mutual willingness to use military escalation and economic disruption in gambits to strengthen positions at the negotiating table. LEBANON An Israeli airstrike Thursday killed two people in southern Lebanon, despite negotiations in Rome to end the conflict between Israel and Hizbollah. The latter rejects the Israeli-Lebanese talks, arguing that Lebanon should instead rely on the group’s patron, Iran, to secure a genuine ceasefire and Israeli troop withdrawal as part of a broader deal with the U.S. This position notwithstanding, Hizbollah has largely halted its own military operations in recent weeks. While Israel has reduced the intensity of its attacks, it persists in conducting lethal strikes in the south, where it continues to occupy territory. Crisis Group expert David Wood says the continued Israeli assaults undermine the historic direct diplomacy that is happening between Israeli and Lebanese officials. Left unchecked, Israel’s attacks could sour relations between Tehran and Washington even further, making it even more difficult to reverse the escalatory cycle that has taken off in the Gulf. 10 July 2026 ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE UN Secretary-General António Guterres opened the Global Dialogue on AI Governance in Geneva Monday by reiterating a call for a ban on what are called Lethal Autonomous Weapon Systems, arguing that “some decisions must remain forever human – none more than taking a human life”. Crisis Group expert Issandr El Amrani says it is urgent to regulate the use of AI in warfare: AI-aided weapon systems are enabling rapid processing of targets with decreased human oversight, with potentially grave consequences for civilians, as seen during Israel’s war in Gaza and the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran. These “killer robots” need not be fully autonomous to render human oversight largely meaningless. More than 120 states, mostly from the Global South, have endorsed such a ban. But countries that have this technology, including the U.S., the UK and Russia, oppose it, contending that current provisions under international humanitarian law are sufficient. CHINA China test-fired a long-range ballistic missile from a nuclear-powered submarine in the South Pacific Monday, its first such exercise in these waters in two years. Beijing characterised the missile test as part of routine annual training that comports with international law, stressing that it was not directed at another country. Australia, Japan and New Zealand raised objections, however, with Australian Foreign Minister Penny Wong calling the test “destabilising” for the Asia Pacific and Japanese Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara describing it as “a grave concern” for the world. Crisis Group expert William Yang says the test sends a signal to the U.S. and allies that Beijing is determined to push back against what it views as attempts to contain China’s rise. The test took place on the same day that Australia signed a mutual defence agreement with Fiji. It will likely push other Asia Pacific countries both to deepen such cooperation and to accelerate their own military modernisation. SOUTH SUDAN On Sunday, opposition fighters killed James Kueth Makuach, commissioner of Akobo county in Jonglei state, in what President Salva Kiir’s government described as an “assassination”. Makuach had belonged to the party of former Vice President Riek Machar, who was arrested on sedition charges last year amid fighting between his loyalists and government forces. In April, Makuach defected to Kiir’s camp. The president then reappointed him as county commissioner, breaching South Sudan’s 2018 peace accord, which allotted this post to Machar’s group. Crisis Group expert Daniel Akech says the Akobo attack, which also took the lives of two other government officials, is part of an escalation in clashes in Jonglei over the past week. But it appears to have been an act of political retribution rather than a push for territory or another military objective. Makuach’s killing underscores the dangers of proceeding with national elections planned for December with no political consensus in Juba and swathes of the country embroiled in civil strife. 3 July 2026 AFGHANISTAN - PAKISTAN Tensions between Afghanistan and Pakistan flared again this week. On Sunday, Pakistani forces once again carried out strikes across the border in Afghanistan, saying they killed 29 militants. Islamabad said the strikes were retaliation for recent attacks inside Pakistan, including a Karachi assault that killed three security personnel. According to the UN, at least 28 civilians were killed and another 49 injured in the strikes. Pakistan accuses the Afghan Taliban of sheltering anti-Pakistan militants, which Taliban officials deny. On Wednesday, Afghanistan said it carried out strikes inside Pakistan, targeting ISIS and other armed opposition groups. Islamabad denies Taliban accusations of harbouring such groups and noted that it had intercepted four drones launched from Afghan territory. Crisis Group expert Ibraheem Bahiss says outside mediators should push the sides toward practical border and security arrangements before the cycle of strikes and counterstrikes escalates further. NIGERIA Violence is again escalating in north-western Nigeria. Long plagued by bandits who engage in mass kidnappings for ransom, pillage and extortion, the region is also now seeing increased jihadist activity. Together, bandit and jihadist attacks killed over 150 people in Katsina, Kebbi, Sokoto and Zamfara states in June, a notable uptick from previous months. On 28 May, Islamic State Sahel Province claimed what appears to be its first reported attacks in the region, in which eighteen soldiers and one police officer were killed in Kebbi and Sokoto states. Amid this escalation, on 20 June prominent bandit leader Bello Turji claimed responsibility for deadly attacks on troops and declared his group ready for either peace talks or prolonged war with the government. If the bandit and jihadist threats are not reined in, says Crisis Group expert Nnamdi Obasi, north-western Nigeria could become part of the wider belt of instability in the Sahel. SUDAN Fighting centred on El Obeid, North Kordofan’s state capital, has intensified in recent weeks as drone strikes increase and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) mobilise around the city, raising fears of encirclement and blockade. UN relief chief Tom Fletcher warned Tuesday that El Obeid risks becoming “another El Fasher”, referring to North Darfur’s capital, which endured a prolonged siege before falling to the RSF last October and suffering mass atrocities. Crisis Group expert Shewit Woldemichael says a siege of El Obeid would deepen the humanitarian crisis facing civilians, many of whom have already fled to the city from fighting elsewhere. Meanwhile, the increased use of drones against El Obeid could allow for sustained attacks through the now-beginning rainy season, when ground fighting has typically slowed. 26 June 2026 BOLIVIA President Rodrigo Paz declared a state of exception starting Saturday after more than 50 days of protests triggered by a land reform law and planned austerity measures. Authorities say at least 37 people have been injured in clashes between demonstrators and police. The decree bans the protesters’ roadblocks that have paralysed commercial traffic, causing shortages of basic goods in the administrative capital La Paz, and (temporarily) allows the armed forces to assist police in reopening key routes. It does not, however, suspend fundamental rights, as is often the case with states of exception in Latin America. Before making the declaration, Paz had signed an agreement to “pacify” the country with the biggest trade union, the Bolivian Workers’ Central, which withdrew from the streets. Most of the roadblocks have vanished since the measure took effect. But Crisis Group expert Glaeldys González Calanche says tensions remain high. The unrest could erupt anew if the government fails to deliver on socio-economic commitments it made to the union or if other groups involved in the protests, including campesinos and Indigenous people, decide to resume the pressure. COLOMBIA Right-wing Abelardo de la Espriella won Sunday’s presidential runoff by the thinnest margin in Colombian history, defeating Iván Cepeda, who had campaigned on continuing leftist President Gustavo Petro’s social reform agenda. De la Espriella styles himself as an outsider. Boasting of his ties to U.S. President Donald Trump, who endorsed him before the vote, he has vowed to take an iron-fist approach to organised crime, for instance pledging to bomb narco-traffickers and build mega-prisons. Many Colombians are ready for such measures, says Crisis Group expert Renata Segura, having become frustrated with Petro’s attempts to negotiate “total peace” with criminal and other armed groups. But, as the close vote shows, nearly half the electorate is equally concerned about de la Espriella’s promise to circumvent checks and balances in pursuit of quick fixes. To protect public safety, Colombia needs to balance crimefighting with efforts to plug the gaps in state services that criminal organisations exploit, including for recruitment. The new government should not disregard negotiations, which, if done the right way, have proven an effective tool for reducing violence in Colombia. U.S. - IRAN U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio confirmed Wednesday that technical delegations from the U.S. and Iran will reconvene at the end of June to resume talks aimed at ending the conflict between the two countries. By the terms of the memorandum of understanding reached between the Trump administration and Tehran in Islamabad earlier this month, these working groups are tasked with negotiating the details leading to a “final deal”, including nuclear commitments by Iran and sanctions relief provisions by the U.S. Maintaining momentum in dialogue is critical, says Crisis Group expert Ali Vaez, as the two sides have put forward clashing interpretations of the parameters they agreed to in Pakistan. The negotiations have many moving parts – related to the Strait of Hormuz and Lebanon, among other issues. In this ambitious scope lies promise, but also peril, as a setback on any one front could derail the whole endeavour. 19 June 2026 HAITI Visiting Tuesday, UN Secretary-General António Guterres said Haiti is suffering “the worst humanitarian crisis in the Western Hemisphere”. He toured the headquarters of the new Gang Suppression Force assembled to battle the criminal bands bedevilling the country. The UN released figures showing that gang violence has killed 2,300 people in the year to date and displaced a record 1.5 million more. Gangs have also kidnapped around 100 Haitians, including the defence ministry’s cabinet director last week. Crisis Group expert Diego Da Rin says much hope rests on the new force, but whether it can deliver remains to be seen as it builds toward its mandated strength of 5,500. Gangs, meanwhile, appear to be adapting, attacking senior officials and expanding abductions into formerly safe areas, possibly to deter anti-gang operations where kidnapping victims are held. MYANMAR - CHINA Chinese President Xi Jinping hosted Myanmar’s coup-leader-turned-president Min Aung Hlaing on a state visit to Beijing this week. The two sides reaffirmed their “community with a shared future” and signed eighteen agreements covering areas including transport and development. Crisis Group expert Richard Horsey says the state visit’s symbolism may matter more than any individual deal, as it provides Min Aung Hlaing with a measure of the international legitimacy he craves. For China, meanwhile, it is an opportunity to lock in a dependency that provides growing strategic opportunities, while it pushes for greater calm in conflict-affected areas along the Myanmar border. UKRAINE - RUSSIA Overnight into Thursday, Ukraine launched its largest drone assault on Moscow since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022, hitting an oil refinery and injuring at least seventeen people. Russia said it intercepted 194 drones around Moscow and nearly 1,000 drones and several cruise missiles nationwide over 24 hours. Ukraine said the attack was a response to Russian strikes earlier this week that damaged the UNESCO-listed Kyiv-Pechersk Lavra monastery. Moscow warned it would respond forcefully. Crisis Group expert Lucian Kim says the attacks highlight Ukraine’s efforts to demonstrate it can hit targets far inside Russia using deep-strike drones. But while such attacks create headlines, they have yet to affect the Kremlin’s warfighting ability and may harden support for the war among the Russian public. 12 June 2026 AFGHANISTAN - PAKISTAN Pakistan launched air raids Wednesday across the border with Afghanistan, killing 26 Pakistani Taliban fighters, according to Pakistani Information Minister Attaullah Tarar. The Afghan authorities, however, said the strikes killed thirteen people, including eleven children. The air raids came one day after Pakistani Taliban fighters ambushed a security outpost in Pakistan’s north west, killing six officers. These incidents ended a month of calm in the conflict between the two countries. Crisis Group expert Ibraheem Bahiss says violent flare-ups like these are likely to persist as long as both countries’ security concerns remain unaddressed. IRAN - U.S. The fragile April ceasefire between Washington and Tehran wobbled as the two sides engaged in increasingly sharp exchanges of fire. U.S. forces launched repeated strikes on Iranian targets as Tehran retaliated by targeting U.S. bases in Bahrain, Jordan and Kuwait; Iran and Israel also traded blows for the first time in two months. On Thursday, U.S. President Donald Trump threatened that the U.S. would take control of Kharg island, site of Iran’s main oil terminals, and other energy infrastructure. He backtracked later in the day, cancelling new strikes and insisting that a negotiated deal with Tehran was close. Those talks are likely to be fraught, however, and may not guarantee the end of hostilities if certain issues remain unresolved, such as Israel’s continued attacks on and occupation of over 20 per cent of Lebanon. Crisis Group expert Glaeldys González Calanche says Petro’s claims raise concerns over a peaceful transfer of power if Cepeda loses, while Trump’s involvement has fuelled resentment over foreign interference, which could further trigger demonstrations. The run-off could also test whether Trump’s endorsement helps or hurts candidates elsewhere in the region. CONFLICT-RELATED SEXUAL VIOLENCE The UN on 29 May released its annual report on conflict-related sexual violence, showing that reported cases more than doubled in 2025 after rising 25 per cent the year before. UN Women also recently reported that in Sudan alone, the number of women and girls needing support after sexual violence has quadrupled since civil war broke out three years ago. Crisis Group expert Cristal Downing says survivor services are increasingly scarce after major U.S. aid cuts in 2025 hit programming for which Washington had been the largest donor. Compounding the problem, Washington’s February 2026 “Protecting Human Flourishing in Foreign Assistance” policy restricts aid recipients’ work and speech on abortion. Though the policy’s ban on “promoting” abortion exempts cases of rape, many NGOs fear inconsistent enforcement and unclear compliance requirements, leaving them to choose between U.S. conditions that may limit post-rape care and refusing funding at the risk of jeopardising their wider operations. LEBANON Israel and Lebanon on Wednesday agreed to a new U.S.-brokered ceasefire deal, which would establish pilot zones in southern Lebanon where Hizbollah operatives would be barred. The deal follows a severe Israeli escalation, including its deepest incursion into Lebanese territory in 26 years, which threatened to upset ongoing U.S.-Iran talks. On Thursday, Hizbollah rejected the terms, after Israel said it would continue military operations for now. Unless Israel and Hizbollah both cease fire, however, this latest agreement will soon collapse entirely. 29 May 2026 GAZA Nickolay Mladenov, the Bulgarian diplomat tasked by the U.S.-designed Board of Peace with overseeing the Gaza ceasefire, briefed the UN Security Council last week on his team’s first six months of work. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Friday he has ordered the Israeli army to increase the proportion of Gaza it controls from 60 to 70 per cent, in effect squeezing the strip’s two million people into an even tighter corner. Israeli airstrikes have taken more than 900 Palestinian lives during the ceasefire, including the commander of Hamas’s armed wing and, only days later, his successor, who was killed Wednesday along with his family. Israeli media reported that the Board of Peace had “approved” the assassinations. Crisis Group expert Max Rodenbeck says the Board’s strategy of making relief for Gaza’s people, whether humanitarian aid or broader hopes for the future, conditional on Hamas’s willingness to surrender its arms is deeply troubling and a recipe for prolonging their misery. KOREAN PENINSULA Pyongyang said it tested two new missiles Tuesday, including a short-range, nuclear-capable cruise missile that it plans to deploy with troops facing South Korean soldiers across the Korean peninsula’s demilitarised zone. The same day, Seoul said it had also detected North Korean missile launches toward waters off the peninsula’s western coast. Crisis Group expert Chris Green says the advanced weapon tests will deepen the freeze in peninsular relations, with North Korean leader Kim Jong-un branding South Korea his country’s foremost enemy and pledging to make the border “an impregnable fortress”. Along with Pyongyang’s growing closeness to Moscow and questions about Washington’s commitment to defending South Korea amid its mounting competition with Beijing, the tests are likely to bolster the consensus in Seoul behind more intensive military modernisation of its own. MALI As many as 50 people were killed Wednesday in jihadist raids on two villages in the central Mopti region, underscoring the breadth of the threat posed by the al-Qaeda affiliate Jama’at Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin (JNIM). Meanwhile, JNIM continued to enforce a partial siege of the capital Bamako, preventing scores of trucks bearing fuel and other supplies from reaching the city. Crisis Group expert Jean-Hervé Jezequel says these developments show that weapons continue to do the talking in Mali, even as the situation points to the urgent need for a genuine political dialogue. 22 May 2026 AFGHANISTAN Together with various NGOs, the UN released a plan Tuesday for aiding Afghan refugees expected to return from Iran and Pakistan in the coming months. The UN projects that 2.7 million people will cross back into Afghanistan between April and December. Already, nearly 5.9 million refugees have come back since September 2023, many of them forced to do so by harsh Pakistani visa policies amid rising tensions between Islamabad and the Taliban authorities in Kabul. Now the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran will likely compel many Afghans living in the Islamic Republic to leave, even as the exodus from Pakistan continues. Many of these people are women, who will face draconian Taliban restrictions on freedom of movement and economic activity. The returnees also include children, some of whom have never even been to Afghanistan and will be at greater risk of child marriage, which the Taliban have lately recognised as a legal act. Crisis Group expert Ibraheem Bahiss says international donors should give generously to fund the $529 million UN response plan, without which many returnees will be destitute. NIGERIA The military announced Tuesday that joint strikes carried out with the U.S. had killed 175 jihadist fighters in the preceding week, in addition to destroying stockpiles of arms. The strikes began on 16 May with one that killed Abu Bakr al-Mainuki, deputy leader of the Islamic State-West Africa Province (ISWAP), who had been coordinating activities with jihadists in the Sahelian countries. At a hearing in Washington on Tuesday, General Dagvin Anderson, head of U.S. Africa Command, told U.S. legislators that “the epicentre of global terrorism is in Africa”. The charges relate to a 1996 incident in which Cuban fighter jets shot at planes flown by anti-Castro Cuban Americans trying to help Cubans escape the island. Senior U.S. officials, most recently Central Intelligence Agency head John Ratcliffe, have held a series of semi-secret meetings with high-ranking figures in Havana this spring. Publicly, Cuban leader Miguel Díaz-Canel has remained defiant, rejecting the allegations against Castro as a “political manoeuvre”. Meanwhile, the U.S. has tightened a blockade of Cuba that has precipitated a humanitarian crisis and sent additional warships to the Caribbean Sea. Crisis Group expert Renata Segura says any attempt to forcibly break the tight grip the Cuban Communist Party and military have upon the state could result in violent chaos and further suffering for the Cuban people. 15 May 2026 DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO A spate of lethal violence in the north-eastern Ituri province over the past two weeks has underscored the complexity of the country’s crisis. In late April, a group of Codeco militiamen killed at least 69 people, mainly civilians, in a series of separate attacks. Allied with the Congolese government, Codeco claims to defend the interests of the Lendu people, most of whom are farmers, from encroachment by ethnic Hema herders. According to local sources, it raided several Hema villages in retaliation for assaults on Congolese army positions by a Hema armed group. The following week, gunmen from the Allied Democratic Forces (ADF), a Ugandan insurgency now affiliated with the Islamic State, killed at least fifteen people in Biakato, an Ituri market town. The province has been under martial law since 2021, the same year that Uganda (with Kinshasa’s permission) sent in troops to pursue ADF militants based in Congolese territory. DISPLACEMENT A new report from the Internal Displacement Monitoring Centre shows that armed conflict has become the number-one cause of internal displacement worldwide, surpassing natural disasters, for the first time on record. War and violence drove some 32.3 million people from their homes in 2025, the most ever, representing a 60 per cent increase over 2024. The internal displacements in Iran and the Democratic Republic of Congo made up two thirds of the global total. Crisis Group President and CEO Comfort Ero says these numbers are a sobering reminder of how pervasive conflict has become in today’s world. The human cost of war is never abstract. Preventing war means not just saving lives but also sparing people the pain and distress of being uprooted, often with no certainty of ever going home. Nor did it bring a major reversal, which some in Taiwan had feared, such as Trump agreeing to scale back U.S. arms sales or change Washington’s longstanding declaratory policies toward the island. First, it underscored Trump’s desire to gain a greater foothold in China for U.S. businesses as well as his conviction that a strong working rapport with Xi can produce a cooperative relationship between Washington and Beijing.
